They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.<sup>15</sup>Therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits on the throne will shelter them with his presence.<sup>16</sup>They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat.<sup>17</sup>For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

8.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Four Trumpets
8.overview:
The seventh seal does not release a horseman or a cosmic catastrophe. It releases silence. “When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” After the unceasing worship of chapters 4–7, after the thunder and lightning of the throne room, after the cries of the martyrs and the acclamation of the great multitude — silence. Heaven holds its breath. The silence of the seventh seal is more terrifying than any of the sounds that preceded it, because it signals that something of ultimate gravity is about to happen.

Out of the silence, seven trumpets are given to seven angels. Before the trumpets sound, another angel offers incense before the altar — and the prayers of the saints rise with the incense before God. This is the answer to the martyrs’ prayer of 6:10 (“How long, O Lord?”): the prayers of God’s people are not lost. They have been gathered. They are being presented before the throne. And now fire from the altar is thrown to the earth — the prayers of the saints become the fire of divine judgment.

The trumpets follow the pattern of the Exodus plagues, but escalated. Hail, fire, blood — the first trumpet echoes the seventh plague of Egypt. The sea turning to blood — the second trumpet echoes the first plague. Darkness — the fourth trumpet echoes the ninth plague. The Exodus pattern is deliberate: the God who judged Egypt to liberate his people is now judging the new Egypt (Rome, Babylon) to liberate the new Israel (the church). The judgments of Revelation are not arbitrary cruelties; they are the exodus of the new covenant people on a cosmic scale.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Seventh Seal and the Golden Censer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: the last seal is opened and nothing happens. There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. Everything the reader has heard for four chapters — the ceaseless holy, holy, holy of the living creatures (4:8), the myriads crying Worthy is the Lamb (5:12), a multitude nobody could number (7:10) — stops. Scripture repeatedly commands exactly this silence before God acts in judgment (Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13), and the crowd outside the temple prayed in silence while the incense was offered (Luke 1:10). Both are probably in view.

Verse 2: seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets — the second of the book’s three sevens. A trumpet in Israel sounded at Sinai (Ex. 19:16), brought down Jericho (Josh. 6:16–20), raised the alarm (Joel 2:1), announced Jubilee (Lev. 25:9) and will sound at the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:52).

Verses 3–4: before a trumpet sounds, another angel stands at the altar with a golden censer and is given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints, and the smoke rises before God. This is the payoff of 5:8, where the elders held golden bowls which John identified as those prayers. Three details matter: all the saints; the incense is added from the other side, so the prayers do not go up on their own account; and they arrive.

Verse 5 turns everything over. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, followed by thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake — the Sinai signs of 4:5 with an earthquake added. The same censer that carried the prayers up now carries fire down. The trumpets are the answer to the church’s praying.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer and the Censer

Heaven falls silent, and the prayers of all the saints rise with much incense given at the altar. Then the same censer is filled with fire and thrown to the earth: the trumpets are God’s answer to his people’s prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The martyrs’ “How long?” is being answered.

Now: Prayers that seem to do nothing are gathered, perfected, and answered in God’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, heaven falls silent for about half an hour.

Silence. After ceaseless praise (4:8), a hush: awe before judgment (Habakkuk 2:20; Zephaniah 1:7).

Half an hour. A short, solemn pause.

The seventh seal. It unfolds into the seven trumpets. The end is reached again, from a different angle.

On a Tuesday. God’s silence is not absence. Heaven is listening to prayer (vv. 3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne, and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven angels receive trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar, and the smoke rises before God.

Trumpets. Warning and battle (Joshua 6; Joel 2:1).

The prayers of the saints. Including the martyrs’ cry (6:10). Prayer comes before judgment.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel? Some see Christ, our high priest. Verdict: Revelation never calls Christ an angel; this is an angelic servant. It does not teach that we pray through angels. Our only mediator is Christ (1 Timothy 2:5).

On a Tuesday. Your prayers are not lost. They rise before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it on the earth, bringing thunder, lightning and an earthquake.

Prayers answered. The same altar that received prayer sends judgment. God answers his people’s cries for justice.

Ezekiel 10:2. Coals scattered over the city.

For worship. Praise God that prayer moves history.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6: the seven angels prepare to blow. Verse 7: the first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, and a third of the earth, a third of the trees and all green grass are burned. Verses 8–9: the second brings something like a great mountain, burning, thrown into the sea — the image Jeremiah used of Babylon as a burnt mountain (Jer. 51:25) — and a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of its creatures die, a third of the ships are destroyed. For seven churches on the coast of Asia the sea was the economy, not the scenery.

Verses 10–11: the third trumpet drops a blazing star, Wormwood, on the fresh water, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter. Apsinthos is bitter rather than poisonous, and it is the prophets’ standing image for judgment that makes the sweet unswallowable (Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Lam. 3:19) — most pointedly in Amos, where men turn justice to wormwood (Amos 5:7) and here find their own wells undrinkable.

Verse 12: the fourth strikes a third of the sun, moon and stars, so that a third of the light is darkened — the ninth plague on Egypt (Ex. 10:21–23), aimed at a nation whose chief god was the sun and whose Pharaoh was his son.

Verse 13 closes with an eagle at the zenith, where everyone can see it, crying Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth — one woe for each trumpet still to come. Four trumpets have struck earth, sea, fresh water and sky, the whole created order. The remaining three will fall on people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trumpets Are the Plagues of Egypt

Hail and fire, water turned to blood, bitterness and darkness strike earth, sea, fresh water and sky — each limited to a third. As in Egypt, the aim is to expose false gods and bring God’s people out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For coastal churches, a stricken sea meant a stricken economy.

Now: Do not decode these as headlines; see in them the failure of every false security, and the warning to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them. The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels prepare to blow, and at the first trumpet hail and fire mixed with blood burn up a third of the earth, the trees and the green grass.

The plagues of Egypt. Hail and fire (Exodus 9:23–25). The trumpets echo the exodus: judgment on oppressors, rescue for God’s people.

A third. Partial. The trumpets are warnings calling people to repent (9:20–21).

Where Christians differ: when and how literal? Some apply the trumpets to the fall of Jerusalem or Rome, others to a future tribulation. Verdict: they are symbolic pictures of God’s partial judgments on the world throughout the age between Christ’s comings, warning of the final judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The trumpet plagues echo the plagues on Egypt, but each strikes only a third — judgment still held back.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the second trumpet a burning mountain is thrown into the sea, a third of the sea becomes blood, a third of sea creatures die and a third of ships are destroyed.

The Nile turned to blood. Exodus 7:20.

A burning mountain. Perhaps a picture of a fallen kingdom (Jeremiah 51:25, of Babylon).

Ships. Trade and commerce are struck (compare 18:17–19).

verseByVerse.quote: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water. The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the third trumpet a blazing star called Wormwood falls on a third of the rivers and springs, making them bitter, and many die.

Wormwood. A bitter plant, used by Jeremiah of the bitterness of judgment (Jeremiah 9:15).

Bitter water. The reverse of Marah, where God made bitter water sweet (Exodus 15:23–25).

On a Tuesday. What the world drinks to satisfy it turns bitter without God.
verseByVerse.note: Wormwood is a bitter plant, used by the prophets as a picture of bitter judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night. Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fourth trumpet a third of the sun, moon and stars are darkened, and an eagle cries woe on the earth’s inhabitants because of the three trumpets still to come.

Darkness. The ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23).

Woe, woe, woe. The last three trumpets are worse: they strike people directly.

Those who dwell on the earth. In Revelation, this means unbelievers, whose home and hope are in this world.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “angel” rather than “eagle”. The words are similar in Greek; “eagle” is earlier and better attested.

For worship. Thank God that his warnings come before his final judgment.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.<sup>2</sup>Then I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.<sup>3</sup>And another angel came and stood at the altar with a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before the throne,<sup>4</sup>and the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rose before God from the hand of the angel.<sup>5</sup>Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth, and there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.<sup>6</sup>Now the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared to blow them.<sup>7</sup>The first angel blew his trumpet, and there followed hail and fire, mixed with blood, and these were thrown upon the earth. And a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all green grass was burned up.<sup>8</sup>The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood.<sup>9</sup>A third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.<sup>10</sup>The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.<sup>11</sup>The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the water, because it had been made bitter.<sup>12</sup>The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of their light might be darkened, and a third of the day might be kept from shining, and likewise a third of the night.<sup>13</sup>Then I looked, and I heard an eagle crying with a loud voice as it flew directly overhead, “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, at the blasts of the other trumpets that the three angels are about to blow!”

9.title: The Fifth and Sixth Trumpets: The Demonic and the Deadly
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is among the most vivid and terrifying in Revelation. The fifth trumpet releases demonic locusts from the abyss — creatures drawn from Joel 2 and shaped like scorpions, with the faces of humans and the hair of women and the teeth of lions. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the great Euphrates river, who command an army of two hundred million mounted troops. The devastation escalates from the bounded third of the earlier trumpets to something more comprehensive and more personal: now humanity itself is directly targeted.

The two woe-trumpets of chapter 9 share a common theme: demonic power unleashed. The fifth trumpet releases the army of the abyss, led by “the angel of the bottomless pit” whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon — “Destroyer.” The sixth releases an army from beyond the Euphrates — the frontier from which Israel’s ancient enemies (Assyria, Babylon) had always come. The locust-army of the fifth trumpet torments but does not kill; the cavalry of the sixth kills a third of humanity. The escalation is purposeful: God is turning up the pressure on a world that refuses to repent.

The chapter’s most sobering verse is its final one: “The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent.” The purpose of the trumpet judgments — like the purpose of the Exodus plagues — was to break the hardness of heart that keeps humanity from turning to God. Pharaoh’s hardness repeated in every generation: even faced with the unmistakable signs of divine judgment, even watching a third of their companions die, the survivors “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons.” The judgment does not automatically produce repentance; only grace can break what judgment cannot.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Fifth Trumpet: The Locusts from the Abyss
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a star fallen from heaven — a perfect participle, an event already complete — who is immediately a he, and who was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opens it, and before anything comes out the light goes: smoke like the smoke of a great furnace darkens the sun and the air (cf. Gen. 19:28).

Verses 3–4: locusts come up out of the smoke with the power of scorpions — and are told not to touch grass, plant or tree, which is the one thing locusts exist to do. Their only target is those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads: the first cash-out of chapter 7, and the doorpost of the Exodus Passover moved from the house to the person (cf. Ex. 8:22; 10:23).

Verses 5–6: they are allowed to torment for five months — about the life cycle of a locust swarm — but not to kill. And then the hardest sentence in the chapter: people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them (cf. Job 3:21; Jer. 8:3).

Verses 7–10 describe them in eight comparisons, each introduced by like: horses prepared for battle (Joel 2:4), what looked like crowns of gold, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth (Joel 1:6), iron breastplates, wings like many chariots, and scorpion tails in which their power to hurt resides.

Verses 11–12: Proverbs 30:27 says locusts have no king; these have one — the angel of the bottomless pit, named in both languages, Abaddon (Hebrew for destruction, Job 26:6; 28:22; Prov. 15:11) and Apollyon (Greek for destroyer). Then a line of bookkeeping: the first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
On a Permission

A fallen star is given the key to the abyss; the locusts are told whom they may not touch and allowed five months. Their king is Abaddon, Apollyon, the destroyer — a creature on a leash, not God’s rival.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torment fell on those without God’s seal, and it ended when the season ended.

Now: If you have longed to die, you are in the company of Job, Moses and Elijah, not under condemnation — tell another believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And the fifth angel blew his trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. He opened the shaft of the bottomless pit, and from the shaft rose smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and the air were darkened with the smoke from the shaft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the bottomless pit and opens it, releasing smoke that darkens the sky.

A fallen star. Where Christians differ. Satan (Luke 10:18; Isaiah 14:12), a fallen angel, or a good angel sent from heaven (20:1). Verdict: probably Satan or one of his angels, though either way the key is given to him. Even the abyss opens only by God’s permission.

The bottomless pit. The abyss, the prison of demons (Luke 8:31).

Smoke. Darkness and confusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then from the smoke came locusts on the earth, and they were given power like the power of scorpions of the earth. They were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any green plant or any tree, but only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the smoke come locusts with scorpion power, ordered to harm only people without God’s seal on their foreheads.

Locusts. The eighth plague (Exodus 10), and Joel’s locust army (Joel 1–2).

Not the grass. These are not real locusts. They attack people, not plants: demonic forces.

Only those without the seal. God’s people are protected from this torment (7:3).

For worship. Thank God that his seal protects you from the powers of darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: They were allowed to torment them for five months, but not to kill them, and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings someone. And in those days people will seek death and will not find it. They will long to die, but death will flee from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts may torment but not kill for five months, and people will long to die but death will flee them.

Five months. The lifespan of a locust: limited.

Seek death. The despair of life without God, under the oppression of evil.

What it does not mean. If you are a believer who has longed not to wake up, this verse is not your condemnation. You are sealed. Tell someone, and seek help.
verseByVerse.note: Five months is roughly the life span of a locust, or the season in which they swarm.

verseByVerse.quote: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle: on their heads were what looked like crowns of gold; their faces were like human faces, their hair like women's hair, and their teeth like lions' teeth; they had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the noise of their wings was like the noise of many chariots with horses rushing into battle. They have tails and stings like scorpions, and their power to hurt people for five months is in their tails.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts look like war horses with crowns, human faces, women’s hair, lions’ teeth, iron breastplates and scorpion tails, and their wings roar like chariots.

A nightmare picture. Joel 1:6; 2:4–5. Each detail adds menace: power, intelligence, seduction, ferocity.

What it does not mean. Not attack helicopters or modern weapons, as some popular writers suggest. John describes demonic oppression in Joel’s images, not machines.

verseByVerse.quote: They have as king over them the angel of the bottomless pit. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon. The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are still to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their king is the angel of the abyss, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, and the first woe is past.

Destroyer. Both names mean destruction. Satan destroys; Christ saves.

Apollyon. Some see a play on Apollo, a god whose symbols included the locust and whom some emperors claimed as patron.

On a Tuesday. The devil’s aim is always destruction. Know your enemy.
verseByVerse.note: Abaddon means “destruction” and Apollyon “destroyer.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Sixth Trumpet: The Army from the Euphrates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 13–14: the sixth trumpet, and a voice from the four horns of the golden altar — the incense altar, where the prayers of all the saints were offered in 8:3–4 and from which fire was thrown down in 8:5. The order it gives is Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates. They are bound; they must be released; the order comes from the altar where the church prays. The Euphrates was the empire’s eastern frontier and the direction every invasion of Israel had come from.

Verse 15: the four had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year — one article in the Greek governs all four, so this is a fixed moment rather than a duration — and are released to kill a third of mankind. The fraction has moved from things to people. Verse 16 gives the number of mounted troops as twice ten thousand times ten thousand, with the telling clause I heard their number, exactly as at 7:4.

Verses 17–19: breastplates the colour of fire, sapphire and sulfur — the same three things the horses breathe. Lions’ heads; fire, smoke and sulfur from their mouths, the substance of Sodom (Gen. 19:24) and of the lake of fire (19:20; 20:10). A third of mankind killed by these three plagues. And the power is in mouths and in tails, the tails being like serpents with heads — the word John reserves for the dragon (12:9; 20:2).

Verses 20–21 give the verdict the whole sequence was building toward. The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent — not of the works of their hands, not of worshipping demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood which cannot see or hear or walk (Ps. 115:4–8), and not of their murders, sorceries, sexual immorality or thefts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Comes from the Altar

The voice that releases the four angels comes from the altar where the saints’ prayers are offered. They were prepared for the hour, day, month and year. Yet the survivors did not repent of their idols, sorceries and sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beyond the Euphrates lay the invader every Roman province feared.

Now: Judgement alone does not change hearts; we become like what we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the sixth angel blew his trumpet, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the sixth trumpet a voice from the golden altar orders the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates.

The golden altar. The altar of the saints’ prayers (8:3). Judgment answers prayer.

The Euphrates. The frontier from which Israel’s invaders came (Assyria, Babylon), and Rome’s feared Parthians.

Bound. These evil angels act only when released.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “four” before “horns”.
verseByVerse.note: The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman world, beyond which lay the feared Parthians.

verseByVerse.quote: So the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, were released to kill a third of mankind. The number of mounted troops was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four angels, prepared for that exact hour, are released to kill a third of mankind, with an army of two hundred million horsemen.

The hour, day, month and year. God’s timing is exact.

Two hundred million. A number beyond counting.

What it does not mean. Not a modern army from a particular nation. This is a demonic host, pictured as a vast cavalry.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is how I saw the horses in my vision and those who rode them: they wore breastplates the color of fire and of sapphire and of sulfur, and the heads of the horses were like lions' heads, and fire and smoke and sulfur came out of their mouths. By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur coming out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails, for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by means of them they wound.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The horses and riders wear breastplates of fire, sapphire and sulphur, with lion heads breathing fire, smoke and sulphur, and tails like serpents.

Fire, smoke and sulphur. The marks of hell and of Sodom (Genesis 19:24; 14:10).

Power in mouth and tail. Front and back: no escape.

verseByVerse.quote: The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols of gold and silver and bronze and stone and wood, which cannot see or hear or walk, nor did they repent of their murders or their sorceries or their sexual immorality or their thefts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of mankind, not killed by these plagues, still did not repent of worshipping demons and idols, nor of their murders, sorceries, immorality and thefts.

No repentance. Like Pharaoh, they harden themselves. Judgment alone does not change the heart.

Demons and idols. Behind idols stand demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).

Sorceries. Pharmakeia: magic and spells, not medicine.

The purpose of the trumpets. They were meant to bring repentance. God is patient (2 Peter 3:9).

On a Tuesday. Respond to God’s warnings while there is time.

For worship. Pray for those who have not repented.
