10.title: The Angel and the Little Scroll
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the second great interlude of Revelation — this one inserted between the sixth and seventh trumpets (as chapter 7 was inserted between the sixth and seventh seals). The interlude performs the same function: it pauses the judgment sequence to reorient the reader to the prophetic commission of the church. Before the seventh trumpet sounds and the final woe arrives, John is given a little scroll to eat and recommissioned to prophesy.

A mighty angel descends from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun, his legs like pillars of fire — imagery that deliberately echoes the description of Christ in chapter 1. He stands on sea and land (claiming sovereignty over the whole earth), holds a little open scroll, and cries out with a loud voice like a lion’s roar. Seven thunders respond — and John is told not to write what the thunders said. This is the only thing in Revelation that is sealed rather than revealed: some of God’s purposes remain hidden until their time.

John eats the little scroll at the angel’s command. It is sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach — an echo of Ezekiel’s commissioning (Ezekiel 2:8–3:3) and Jeremiah’s experience of the word (Jeremiah 15:16). The word of God is sweet to receive — it is the good news of grace, the promise of the kingdom, the comfort of the gospel. But the prophetic task is bitter: to speak God’s word to a world that does not want to hear it, to witness to the truth in the face of hostility, to suffer for the testimony of Jesus. The whole book of Revelation is this little scroll: sweet with the glory of the Lamb, bitter with the suffering of faithful witness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Angel and the Little Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six trumpets have sounded; the seventh does not sound until 11:15. Everything between is an interlude, exactly as chapter 7 stood between the sixth and seventh seals — a repetition that is itself an argument about how John builds his sevens.

Verses 1–2: another mighty angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire — every detail borrowed from the descriptions of God and of Christ (1:7, 15, 16; 4:3; Ex. 13:21). He holds a little scroll, and it is already open, unlike the sealed scroll of chapter 5. He sets his right foot on the sea and his left on the land: the conqueror’s posture (Josh. 1:3), with one foot on each of the two places the beasts of chapter 13 will rise from.

Verse 3: he calls out like a lion roaring — the prophets’ image for God speaking (Amos 3:8; Hos. 11:10; Joel 3:16) — and the seven thunders sound, the definite article suggesting a known set, most likely the sevenfold voice of the LORD in Psalm 29. Verse 4: John, pen in hand and about to write, is stopped: Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.

Verses 5–7: the angel raises his right hand and swears — the posture of Daniel 12:6–7 — by the one who lives for ever and who made heaven, earth and sea, that there would be no more delay, and that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.

Verses 8–10: John is sent to take the open scroll and told Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey — Ezekiel’s commission exactly (Ezek. 2:9–3:3; cf. Jer. 15:16). He eats, and reports the tastes in the order he met them: sweet first, bitter after. Verse 11 sends him back to work: You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sealed Thunders and the Swallowed Scroll

A mighty angel in his master’s glory stands on sea and land. What the seven thunders said is sealed — the one sealed sentence in an unsealed book. The angel swears there will be no more delay, and John must eat the little scroll: sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An exiled old man was recommissioned to prophesy to peoples, nations and kings.

Now: Do not claim to know what God has withheld; and expect the gospel to be sweet to receive and costly to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire. He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mighty angel, clothed in cloud and rainbow, with a face like the sun, comes down holding an open little scroll and plants his feet on sea and land.

An interlude. As between the sixth and seventh seals (chapter 7), so between the sixth and seventh trumpets: a pause to show the church’s calling.

Where Christians differ: is this angel Christ? His features recall Christ in chapter 1. Verdict: Revelation never calls Christ an angel, and this one swears by God (v. 6). He is a mighty angel who reflects Christ’s glory as his messenger.

Sea and land. Authority over the whole earth, where the beasts will rise (13:1, 11).

A little scroll, open. Probably the message of the great scroll of chapter 5, now given to John to proclaim.

verseByVerse.quote: and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded. And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel roars like a lion and the seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said and not write it.

Sealed. The only time John is told not to write. God has not told us everything.

Deuteronomy 29:29. The secret things belong to God; what is revealed belongs to us.

What it does not mean. Not an invitation to speculate about what the thunders said. No one can claim to know.

On a Tuesday. Be content with what God has revealed, and obey it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay, but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay: at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God, announced to the prophets, will be fulfilled.

Daniel 12:7. An angel raised his hands and swore by him who lives for ever. There the question was “how long?”; here the answer is “no more delay.”

The mystery of God. His plan to save his people and judge evil, now completed.

The good news to his servants. God’s purposes were announced in advance.

For worship. The martyrs asked “how long?” (6:10). God has answered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, "Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land." So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, "Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey." And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told to take the little scroll and eat it; it is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach.

Ezekiel 2:8–3:3. The prophet eats God’s word before he speaks it.

Sweet then bitter. God’s word is sweet to receive (Psalm 19:10), but bitter in what it contains and costs: judgment for the world and suffering for its messengers.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s word in deeply before you speak it. Expect both sweetness and cost.
verseByVerse.note: Like Ezekiel, John eats God’s message: sweet to receive, bitter because it announces judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was told, "You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings.

Again. John’s commission is renewed. The rest of the book follows.

To the nations. The church’s witness to the world (chapter 11).

For worship. Thank God that his word still goes out to all nations, and pray for those who carry it.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, and his face was like the sun, and his legs like pillars of fire.<sup>2</sup>He had a little scroll open in his hand. And he set his right foot on the sea, and his left foot on the land,<sup>3</sup>and called out with a loud voice, like a lion roaring. When he called out, the seven thunders sounded.<sup>4</sup>And when the seven thunders had sounded, I was about to write, but I heard a voice from heaven saying, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.”<sup>5</sup>And the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven<sup>6</sup>and swore by him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and what is in it, the earth and what is in it, and the sea and what is in it, that there would be no more delay,<sup>7</sup>but that in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.<sup>8</sup>Then the voice that I had heard from heaven spoke to me again, saying, “Go, take the scroll that is open in the hand of the angel who is standing on the sea and on the land.”<sup>9</sup>So I went to the angel and told him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, “Take and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”<sup>10</sup>And I took the little scroll from the hand of the angel and ate it. It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.<sup>11</sup>And I was told, “You must again prophesy about many peoples and nations and languages and kings.”

11.title: The Two Witnesses and the Seventh Trumpet
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is the most compressed chapter in Revelation, covering the entire church age from two angles: the measuring of the temple (the church’s preservation), the ministry of the two witnesses (the church’s prophetic witness), their death and resurrection (the church’s apparent defeat and vindication), and the seventh trumpet (the declaration of the kingdom consummated). It is also one of the most contested chapters in the book.

The measuring of the temple in vv. 1–2 has generated enormous debate. Dispensationalists understand it as a prophecy of a literal rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the tribulation, the outer court given over to Gentile domination for 42 months. The amillennial reading understands the temple as the church (following Paul’s regular use of temple-language for the believing community — 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and the measuring as God’s preservation of his people. The outer court “given over to the nations” represents the church’s visible vulnerability to worldly power — it will be trampled — while the inner sanctuary (the true community of the redeemed) is preserved.

The two witnesses of vv. 3–13 are the most important image in the chapter. Their identity has been debated endlessly: Moses and Elijah (because of the specific powers: turning water to blood = Moses, shutting the sky = Elijah), Elijah and Enoch (the two who did not die), or — the majority Reformed reading — the whole witnessing church across the church age. The number two is the number of legal testimony (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15; Matthew 18:16); the two witnesses represent the complete testimony of the church to the gospel of Jesus Christ. Their supernatural powers (fire from their mouths, power over rain and waters) are the powers of the prophetic word: proclamation that both judges and saves.

The seventh trumpet of vv. 15–19 does not release a new woe but sounds the final declaration of the kingdom: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” This is the answer to the Lord’s Prayer (“Your kingdom come”) and the goal toward which all of history moves. The kingdom is announced as already accomplished — the aorist tense of the verb (“has become”) indicates a completed action. What will still unfold in chapters 12–22 is the working out of what has already been declared from the throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple, the altar and the worshippers — but expressly not the outer court, which is given over to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Measuring in the prophets is a legal owner marking out what is his (Ezek. 40–42; Zech. 2:1–5). Something is claimed and something is deliberately left out, and both are God’s decision.

Verses 3–4: two witnesses are granted authority to prophesy 1,260 days in sackcloth — the coarse black goat hair of mourning, not the uniform of a triumphant movement. They are the two olive trees and the two lampstands of Zechariah 4, where two olive trees feed oil straight into a lampstand and the governing word is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (Zech. 4:6).

Verses 5–6 give their powers, and they are two men’s résumés side by side: fire from the mouth (cf. Jer. 5:14), shutting the sky so that no rain falls — Elijah, for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; Luke 4:25) — and turning water to blood and striking with plagues, which is Moses in Egypt (Ex. 7:17–20).

Verses 7–8: when they have finished their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit makes war on them, conquers them and kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. John supplies the interpretive key himself: pneumatikōs, symbolically. Verses 9–10: for three and a half days the world gazes at the bodies, refuses them burial, and throws the only party in the book — making merry and exchanging presents, because these two prophets had been a torment.

Verses 11–12: a breath of life from God enters them and they stand on their feet (Ezek. 37:10), and a loud voice says Come up here! — the words spoken to John at 4:1 — and they go up in a cloud and their enemies watched them. Verse 13: an earthquake takes a tenth of the city and seven thousand people, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. Verse 14 closes the section: the second woe has passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Measured, Trampled, Raised

God measures his temple and leaves the outer court to be trampled for a bounded time. His two witnesses prophesy in sackcloth, are killed when their testimony is finished, lie unburied while the world celebrates, and are raised and called up in their enemies’ sight.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Plagues had not moved the world; the witnesses’ death and vindication did.

Now: No faithful witness is cut off before his testimony is finished, and a witness that troubles nobody may not be one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, "Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told to measure God’s temple, altar and worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations to trample for forty-two months.

Measuring. A sign of protection and ownership (Ezekiel 40–42; Zechariah 2:1–5).

Where Christians differ: which temple? Futurists see a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem in a future tribulation. Verdict: in the New Testament God’s temple is his people (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21). The church is spiritually protected even while outwardly trampled.

Forty-two months. Three and a half years, Daniel’s “time, times and half a time” (Daniel 7:25). In Revelation it is the period of the church’s suffering witness (12:6, 14; 13:5).

Textual note. A few manuscripts read “within” rather than “outside” the temple.
verseByVerse.note: Forty-two months, 1,260 days (v. 3) and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14) are all three and a half years — Daniel’s limited time of trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth." These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s two witnesses will prophesy for 1,260 days in sackcloth; they are the two olive trees and lampstands before the Lord.

Where Christians differ: who are the two witnesses? Moses and Elijah, Enoch and Elijah, two future prophets, or the church in its witness. Verdict: they are called lampstands, which in Revelation means churches (1:20). They picture the church in its prophetic witness. Two, because two witnesses establish testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15).

Sackcloth. A call to repentance.

Zechariah 4. The olive trees and lampstand: witness by God’s Spirit, not human might.

Where Christians differ: 1,260 days. Futurists take it literally. Verdict: the same period as v. 2, the age of the church’s witness.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed. They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The witnesses are protected until their work is done: fire destroys their enemies, and they can shut the sky and strike the earth with plagues.

Elijah and Moses. Elijah shut the sky (1 Kings 17:1) and called down fire (2 Kings 1:10). Moses turned water to blood.

Fire from their mouth. The word of God (Jeremiah 5:14).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should harm their enemies. The power is God’s word, which judges those who reject it.
verseByVerse.note: Their powers recall Elijah (fire, drought) and Moses (water to blood, plagues).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them, and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When their testimony is finished, the beast from the abyss kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city where their Lord was crucified.

When they have finished. They cannot die before their work is done.

The beast. Introduced fully in chapter 13.

The great city. Spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where Christ was crucified. Not just Jerusalem, but the world in rebellion against God (16:19; 17:18).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “our Lord” for “their Lord”.

verseByVerse.quote: For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb, and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For three and a half days the nations gaze at their bodies and refuse burial, and the world celebrates and sends gifts, because these prophets had tormented them.

No burial. A final insult.

Celebration. The world’s relief at a silenced conscience.

Three and a half days. Short, compared to the 1,260 days of witness.

On a Tuesday. When the church seems defeated, the story is not over.

verseByVerse.quote: But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them. Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, "Come up here!" And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three and a half days God’s breath of life enters them, they stand up, and they go up to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch.

Ezekiel 37:10. Breath enters the dry bones.

Like Christ. Death, resurrection and ascension. The church follows its Lord.

Come up here. The vindication of God’s people before the world.

For worship. Praise God that his witnesses are vindicated.

verseByVerse.quote: And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven. The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great earthquake strikes the city, seven thousand die, and the rest are terrified and give glory to God; the second woe is past.

A tenth and seven thousand. Judgment is again limited.

Where Christians differ: genuine conversion? Some read it as mere terror, others as true repentance. Verdict: to give glory to God is the language of repentance (14:7; 16:9). Through the church’s witness and vindication, many turn to God. A reversal of Elijah’s seven thousand (1 Kings 19:18): there seven thousand were spared, here nine-tenths.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 15: the seventh trumpet sounds and brings no plague at all, only an announcement — The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Singular kingdom, not plural: one worldly system under many governments, and it has changed hands. And the verb is aorist, a completed act: not will become but has become.

Verses 16–17: the twenty-four elders come off their own thrones onto their faces, giving thanks to Lord God Almighty, who is and who was — and the threefold title of 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8 has lost its third term. The one who is to come has come, and the future tense drops out of the name of God. You have taken your great power and begun to reign: not been given, but taken. He was always sovereign; what changes is that the reign becomes visible and unopposed.

Verse 18 quotes Psalm 2:1 in the past tense — the nations raged, and it is over — and lists what the moment contains: wrath; the dead judged; the servants rewarded, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great; and destroying the destroyers of the earth, an exact reciprocity using the same root twice.

Verse 19 opens the temple in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple — the object that stood behind the veil, seen by one man once a year, and lost when Babylon destroyed the temple in 586 BC. Then the storm signs, now five of them: lightning, rumblings, thunder, earthquake and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kingdom Has Come

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. God is now praised as the one who is and who was — the one to come has come — and the ark of his covenant is seen in his temple.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outcome was declared with eleven chapters still to run.

Now: Believers live inside a victory already won and not yet seen; small and great alike will be rewarded.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever." And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God, saying, "We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven declares that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign for ever.

Has become. Announced as done.

The end again. The seventh trumpet brings us to the final reign of God.

Who is and who was. No longer “who is to come”, because he has come.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “and who is to come” in v. 17.

For worship. Sing it, as Handel set it: he shall reign for ever and ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth." Then God's temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations raged, but God’s wrath has come, the time to judge the dead, reward his servants and destroy the destroyers; and God’s temple opens, revealing the ark of the covenant.

Psalm 2. The nations rage, God reigns.

Small and great. All rewarded, whatever their status.

Destroying the destroyers. Judgment is God’s justice on those who ruined his earth.

The ark. Lost since the Babylonian exile, now seen in heaven. God’s covenant presence was never lost.

On a Tuesday. Fear God’s name, and serve him. He rewards.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff, and I was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there,<sup>2</sup>but do not measure the court outside the temple; leave that out, for it is given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.<sup>3</sup>And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth.”<sup>4</sup>These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth.<sup>5</sup>And if anyone would harm them, fire pours from their mouth and consumes their foes. If anyone would harm them, this is how he is doomed to be killed.<sup>6</sup>They have the power to shut the sky, that no rain may fall during the days of their prophesying, and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague, as often as they desire.<sup>7</sup>And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the bottomless pit will make war on them and conquer them and kill them,<sup>8</sup>and their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city that symbolically is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.<sup>9</sup>For three and a half days some from the peoples and tribes and languages and nations will gaze at their dead bodies and refuse to let them be placed in a tomb,<sup>10</sup>and those who dwell on the earth will rejoice over them and make merry and exchange presents, because these two prophets had been a torment to those who dwell on the earth.<sup>11</sup>But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.<sup>12</sup>Then they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them, “Come up here!” And they went up to heaven in a cloud, and their enemies watched them.<sup>13</sup>And at that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand people were killed in the earthquake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven.<sup>14</sup>The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe is soon to come.<sup>15</sup>Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.”<sup>16</sup>And the twenty-four elders who sit on their thrones before God fell on their faces and worshiped God,<sup>17</sup>saying, “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign.<sup>18</sup>The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants, the prophets and saints, and those who fear your name, both small and great, and for destroying the destroyers of the earth.”<sup>19</sup>Then God’s temple in heaven was opened, and the ark of his covenant was seen within his temple. There were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail.

12.title: The Woman, the Dragon, and the War in Heaven
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is the theological heart of Revelation. Everything that has come before — the seals, the trumpets, the witnesses — and everything that follows — the beasts, the bowls, Babylon’s fall — is explained here. We are shown the cosmic backstory: the war between the dragon and the woman, the birth of the child who will rule all nations, the war in heaven that cast Satan down, and the dragon’s fury against the woman’s offspring. This is the explanation for why the church is persecuted: the dragon, having failed to destroy the child, turns his fury on those who “hold to the testimony of Jesus.”

The great sign in heaven — the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars — draws on Genesis 37:9 (Joseph’s dream where the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, representing his family) and on the Old Testament imagery of Israel as the bride/mother of God’s people (Isaiah 54; Jeremiah 6:2). The woman is not Mary (though the imagery encompasses the incarnation). She is the messianic community — Israel who gave birth to the Messiah, and the church who is the continuation and expansion of that community. She is clothed with cosmic glory; she is in labor.

The great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns and seven diadems is Satan himself, identified explicitly in v. 9: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.” His seven heads and ten horns anticipate the beast of chapter 13, which mirrors the dragon’s appearance — the beast is the dragon’s instrument, Rome as the embodiment of satanic opposition to Christ. The dragon’s tail sweeping down a third of the stars has been interpreted as the fall of the angels who followed Satan in the primordial rebellion.

The cosmic war of vv. 7–12 is one of the most dramatic scenes in Revelation: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels; the dragon is thrown down. The war in heaven is won. The announcement that follows is the theological explanation: they conquered “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.” The cross — not Michael’s sword — is the decisive weapon. The dragon is thrown down because the Lamb was slain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman and the Dragon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a great sign — John says so before he describes anything — a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, a crown of twelve stars, pregnant and screaming in labour. The sun, moon and twelve stars come from Joseph’s dream, where Jacob himself supplies the key (Gen. 37:9–10): this is the covenant people, from whom the Messiah comes.

Verses 3–4: another sign, a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven diadems — royal crowns, not the victor’s wreath the woman wears, and the crowns that belong by right to the rider of 19:12. His tail sweeps down a third of the stars, and he stands in front of the woman waiting to devour the child.

Verse 5: she bears a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9) — and the child is caught up to God and to his throne. Between the birth and the throne there is nothing: no Galilee, no cross, no empty tomb. Thirty-three years pass in a comma, because from the dragon’s side there is nothing to report but total failure.

Verse 6: the woman flees into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, to be nourished for 1,260 days. The child is safe on the throne; the mother is in the desert — which is the position of the church between the ascension and the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
The War Behind the War

The woman — the covenant people, Israel and the church — bears the Messiah, while the dragon waits to devour the child. The child is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman is kept and fed in the wilderness for a measured time.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Every attack on the promised line, from Pharaoh to Herod, was the dragon at the woman’s feet.

Now: The church’s wilderness is hard, but it is a place prepared by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars. She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, standing on the moon, crowned with twelve stars, crying out in labour.

A new beginning. Chapters 12–14 go back behind the scenes to show the deeper conflict behind the church’s suffering.

Sun, moon and twelve stars. Joseph’s dream of Jacob’s family (Genesis 37:9). The woman is Israel, God’s people.

Where Christians differ: who is the woman? Roman Catholic tradition sees Mary, crowned as Queen of Heaven. Verdict: the woman is the people of God, Israel bringing forth the Messiah and then the church persecuted (v. 17). Mary belongs within that picture as the mother of Jesus, but the woman is a community, not one person, and the text does not support Marian doctrines.

Birth pains. Israel waiting and suffering for the Messiah (Isaiah 26:17; Micah 5:3).
verseByVerse.note: The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream of Israel’s family. The woman seems to be the people of God, from whom the Messiah came.

verseByVerse.quote: And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems. His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second sign: a great red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven crowns, whose tail sweeps a third of the stars down to earth, stands ready to devour the child when it is born.

The dragon. Named in v. 9: Satan, the ancient serpent.

Seven heads and crowns. A claim to complete power and rule.

A third of the stars. Perhaps angels who fell with him (v. 9), or Daniel 8:10’s picture of an arrogant king.

Ready to devour. Herod’s massacre at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16) was one moment of this.

verseByVerse.quote: She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne, and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman gives birth to a son who will rule the nations, who is caught up to God’s throne, and the woman flees to a place God has prepared in the wilderness for 1,260 days.

The male child. Christ, the king of Psalm 2:9.

Caught up. His whole life, death and resurrection are compressed into his ascension. The dragon failed.

The wilderness. As Israel was fed in the wilderness after the exodus, the church is kept by God in this age.

1,260 days. The same period as 11:3, the age of the church.

For worship. Praise God that the dragon could not devour Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Satan Thrown Down to Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: war in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon and his; the dragon fights back, is defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. Michael appears in Scripture only in Daniel, Jude and here — the great prince who has charge of your people (Dan. 12:1), and the archangel who would not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against the devil but said The Lord rebuke you (Jude 9).

Verse 9 gives him four names in one sentence, and each is a job description: the great dragon, raw destructive power; that ancient serpent, the same one, from the garden; the devil, diabolos, slanderer; and Satan, Hebrew for adversary or accuser. Two of the four mean the same thing. He is also the deceiver of the whole world, and the verb thrown down is repeated three times in the verse.

Verse 10 explains it, and the explanation is a court case: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. Verse 11 defines the book’s central verb in three clauses — they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Verse 12 gives the two reactions: heaven rejoices, earth and sea are warned, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Accuser Thrown Down

Satan, the accuser who stood as prosecutor before God, is thrown down. The saints conquer him by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and by not loving their lives even to death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations that had buried martyrs were told those deaths were victories.

Now: The voice reciting your record has lost its standing, because the charges were paid. His fury is the fury of one whose time is short.

verseByVerse.quote: Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back, but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven. And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, and Satan, the ancient serpent and deceiver of the world, is thrown down to earth with his angels.

Michael. The archangel who protects God’s people (Daniel 12:1).

Five names. Dragon, serpent, devil (slanderer), Satan (accuser), deceiver.

Where Christians differ: when was Satan thrown down? Some place it before creation; futurists place it in a future tribulation. Verdict: the song that follows ties it to the coming of Christ’s kingdom and the blood of the Lamb (vv. 10–11). Satan’s defeat was secured at the cross (John 12:31; Colossians 2:15). Michael’s victory in heaven reflects Christ’s on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, "Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God. And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death. Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven rejoices that God’s kingdom has come and the accuser has been thrown down; believers conquered him by the Lamb’s blood and their testimony, loving not their lives to death; but woe to earth, for the devil has come down in fury, knowing his time is short.

The accuser. Satan accused God’s people day and night (Job 1; Zechariah 3). The cross has silenced him (Romans 8:33–34).

How they conquered. The blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives. Not by force.

His time is short. A defeated enemy is a furious one.

On a Tuesday. When the accuser reminds you of your sins, answer with the blood of the Lamb.

For worship. Praise God that the accuser has been thrown down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Dragon Pursues the Woman
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 13: when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down, he pursued the woman. The logic matters — he goes after the mother because he cannot reach the child, who is on the throne, and cannot go back to the courtroom.

Verse 14: the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle to fly into the wilderness, to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time. The wings are the exodus — I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself (Ex. 19:4; cf. Deut. 32:11; Isa. 40:31) — and the time is Daniel 7:25, the third form of the same number John has now used three ways in two chapters.

Verses 15–16: the serpent pours a river out of his mouth to sweep her away, and the earth came to the help of the woman and swallowed it — as the ground opened on Korah (Num. 16:31–33) and the sea closed over Pharaoh’s chariots.

Verse 17: the dragon, furious, goes off to make war on the rest of her offspring — reaching back to Genesis 3:15 — defined by exactly two marks: those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And the chapter ends on a quiet, ominous line: And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Complete Exodus

Thrown down, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings and carried to the wilderness to be fed. The flood from his mouth is swallowed by the earth, and he turns on her children — those who keep God’s commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The church under Rome was living inside the story of Exodus, and knew how it ended.

Now: Persecution is the rage of a defeated accuser, and the wilderness is where God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thrown down to earth, the dragon pursues the woman, but she is given eagle’s wings to fly to her place in the wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, times and half a time.

Eagle’s wings. Exodus 19:4: God carried Israel out of Egypt on eagles’ wings.

Nourished. The church is persecuted but sustained.

Time, times and half a time. Daniel 7:25. The same period as the 1,260 days.

On a Tuesday. The church is not left to fend for itself. God feeds it.

verseByVerse.quote: The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood. But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent pours a flood to sweep the woman away, but the earth swallows it, so the furious dragon goes off to make war on the rest of her children, who keep God’s commands and hold the testimony of Jesus.

A flood. Perhaps lies and persecution (Psalm 124:4).

The earth helps. Creation itself serves God’s protection, as the earth swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:32).

The rest of her offspring. Christians. The church, the woman, is also her children: individual believers.

Keep God’s commandments. The marks of true believers: obedience and testimony to Jesus.

Textual note. The last sentence reads “he stood on the sand of the sea”, the dragon waiting for the beast to rise. Later manuscripts read “I stood”, which makes it John and places it at the start of chapter 13 (as in the King James Version). “He” is the better reading.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars.<sup>2</sup>She was pregnant and was crying out in birth pains and the agony of giving birth.<sup>3</sup>And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, and on his heads seven diadems.<sup>4</sup>His tail swept down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she bore her child he might devour it.<sup>5</sup>She gave birth to a male child, one who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron, but her child was caught up to God and to his throne,<sup>6</sup>and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, in which she is to be nourished for 1,260 days.<sup>7</sup>Now war arose in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon. And the dragon and his angels fought back,<sup>8</sup>but he was defeated, and there was no longer any place for them in heaven.<sup>9</sup>And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—he was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him.<sup>10</sup>And I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God.<sup>11</sup>And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.<sup>12</sup>Therefore, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them! But woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!”<sup>13</sup>And when the dragon saw that he had been thrown down to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child.<sup>14</sup>But the woman was given the two wings of the great eagle so that she might fly from the serpent into the wilderness, to the place where she is to be nourished for a time, and times, and half a time.<sup>15</sup>The serpent poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman, to sweep her away with a flood.<sup>16</sup>But the earth came to the help of the woman, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth.<sup>17</sup>Then the dragon became furious with the woman and went off to make war on the rest of her offspring, on those who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. And he stood on the sand of the sea.

13.title: The Two Beasts: The Dragon's Earthly Instruments
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the political theology chapter of Revelation. The dragon, standing on the seashore, summons two beasts — one from the sea, one from the land — and delegates to them his authority, his throne, and great power. Together the dragon and the two beasts form a Satanic trinity that parodies the Holy Trinity: the dragon parodies the Father, the beast from the sea parodies the Son (including a parody death and resurrection), and the beast from the land parodies the Spirit (pointing away from itself to the first beast, as the Spirit points away from himself to the Son). The unholy trinity is the political and religious power structure of every totalitarian system that demands ultimate allegiance.

Interpretive flag — The Beast from the Sea: This is the third major structural decision point. The preterist reading identifies the beast as Nero Caesar — and the gematria (numerical value of letters) of “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew adds up to 666. The mortal wound that was healed (v. 3) refers to the Nero redivivus myth: rumors after Nero’s death in AD 68 that he had survived and would return from the east with the Parthian army. The historicist reading has identified the beast with various historical powers including the papacy. The futurist/dispensational reading sees a still-future individual world ruler, a literal Antichrist who will arise in the last days, be given global political power, and demand global worship. The idealist/amillennial reading understands the beast as the pattern of totalitarian political power that demands ultimate allegiance in every age — with Rome as the first-century embodiment and every subsequent empire that makes similar demands as its successor. The idealist position is followed here, while the specific Nero/Rome referent is fully acknowledged as the primary first-century layer.

Interpretive flag — 666: Three readings predominate. (1) Gematria: “Neron Kaisar” in Hebrew letters (nun-resh-vav-nun / qoph-samek-resh) adds to 666; the spelling without the final n adds to 616, which is the reading of some early manuscripts. The specific first-century referent. (2) The number of incompleteness: six is one less than seven (the number of divine completeness); 666 is the triple intensification of falling short of the divine — the beast is humanity at its most grandiose, still falling short of the glory of God. (3) The number of humanity: six was associated with humanity in some traditions (created on the sixth day). The beast is the ultimate expression of humanity’s totalitarian self-divinization. All three readings illuminate the symbol; none is exhaustive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: a beast rises out of the sea with the dragon’s own features — seven heads, ten horns, royal diadems — and blasphemous names on its heads, which is what Roman coins and inscriptions actually gave the emperors. It is like a leopard, with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth: Daniel’s four beasts (Dan. 7:2–7) compressed into one. And the dragon gave it his power, his throne and great authority — the offer Christ refused in the desert (Luke 4:6).

Verses 3–4: one head has a mortal wound that was healed, and the whole earth marvels. The Greek uses the same participle used of the Lamb at 5:6, so the parody is deliberate. The world worships dragon and beast together, chanting Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it? — the song of the exodus (Ex. 15:11) with a different object, and the meaning of the name Michael turned to the wrong address.

Verses 5–6: the beast was given a mouth of haughty and blasphemous words and was allowed authority for forty-two months (cf. Dan. 7:8, 25). It blasphemes God’s name and his dwelling — and John glosses the dwelling himself: that is, those who dwell in heaven.

Verses 7–8: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them, with authority over every tribe and people and language and nation; and all the earth-dwellers worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain. Verses 9–10 turn to the reader: If anyone has an ear, let him hear — captivity to captivity, sword to sword (cf. Jer. 15:2) — Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Sea

The dragon gives the beast his power, throne and authority. It mimics the Lamb’s death and resurrection, wins the world’s worship because it seems unbeatable, and is allowed to speak blasphemies and make war on the saints for forty-two months.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Rome’s emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions.

Now: Worship of power begins as a calculation that resistance is pointless. The saints’ calling is endurance and faith; their names are in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw a beast rising out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, with ten diadems on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads. And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth. And to it the dragon gave his power and his throne and great authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A beast rises from the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, combining leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power, throne and authority.

Daniel 7. Daniel’s four beasts, representing four empires, are rolled into one.

The sea. The restless nations (17:15), and the source of chaos.

Blasphemous names. Emperors were called “lord”, “saviour” and “son of god” on coins and temples.

The dragon gives. As he offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world (Luke 4:5–6).

Where Christians differ: who is the beast? In John’s day, Rome demanding worship. The Reformers saw it in the papacy. Futurists see a final world ruler. Verdict: the beast is the persecuting power of the state set against God, seen first in Rome, recurring through history, and coming to a final climax before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8).
verseByVerse.note: This beast combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 — leopard, bear, lion and the ten-horned beast.

verseByVerse.quote: One of its heads seemed to have a mortal wound, but its mortal wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled as they followed the beast. And they worshiped the dragon, for he had given his authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the beast’s heads seemed mortally wounded but was healed, and the whole world marvelled, followed it and worshipped the dragon and the beast, saying, “Who is like the beast?”

A parody. As though slain (5:6) — the beast imitates the Lamb.

Where Christians differ: the healed wound. Some link it with legends of Nero returning after his suicide; others with the empire’s recovery after the civil wars of AD 68–69. Verdict: the first readers may well have thought of such events, but the point is that evil power keeps reviving and imitates Christ’s resurrection.

Who is like the beast? A parody of Exodus 15:11, “Who is like you, O LORD?”

On a Tuesday. What does your culture marvel at and follow that is not God?

verseByVerse.quote: And the beast was given a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words, and it was allowed to exercise authority for forty-two months. It opened its mouth to utter blasphemies against God, blaspheming his name and his dwelling, that is, those who dwell in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is given a mouth for arrogant blasphemy and authority for forty-two months, and it slanders God, his name, his dwelling and those who dwell in heaven.

Was given. Repeated through the chapter. The beast has only the power God allows.

Forty-two months. The same period as 11:2 and 12:6: the church age.

Daniel 7:8, 25. The little horn that speaks great things.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them. And authority was given it over every tribe and people and language and nation, and all who dwell on earth will worship it, everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast is allowed to make war on the saints and conquer them, and all whose names are not written in the Lamb’s book of life will worship it.

Conquer the saints. Outwardly. Inwardly they conquer by the blood of the Lamb (12:11).

The book of life. Names written before the foundation of the world. God’s election keeps his people from worshipping the beast.

Before the foundation of the world. The Greek allows two readings: the names were written before creation, or the Lamb was slain before creation (in God’s plan). The ESV prefers the first, as in 17:8.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit the first sentence of v. 7 (“it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them”), probably by accident.

For worship. Thank God that your name was written in the Lamb’s book.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has an ear, let him hear: If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be slain with the sword, with the sword must he be slain. Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let anyone with ears hear: those destined for captivity or the sword will meet it; this calls for the endurance and faith of the saints.

Jeremiah 15:2. What God has appointed will come.

Endurance and faith. Not armed resistance, but patient trust (Matthew 26:52).

Textual note. Manuscripts differ: “if anyone is to be slain with the sword” or “if anyone kills with the sword”. The ESV prefers the first.

On a Tuesday. Accept with faith what you cannot change, and keep faithful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–12: a second beast rises out of the earth — the opposite element, so that between them the dragon has the whole world covered. It has two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. Named three times later as the false prophet (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), its entire function is to make the world worship the first beast.

Verses 13–15: it performs great signs, including fire from heaven — Elijah’s credential on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) — and by the signs it is allowed to work it deceives the earth-dwellers, telling them to make an image for the beast. It is allowed to give the image breath so that it speaks and orders the death of anyone who will not worship it. Behind this stands Daniel 3: an image on a plain, an order to bow at a signal, and a furnace — and three men who said But if not (Dan. 3:17–18).

Verses 16–17: it marks all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name. Verse 18 sets the puzzle: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Beast from the Land

A second beast with horns like a lamb and a voice like a dragon makes the world worship the first. It works signs, gives the image a voice, and requires a mark — the beast’s name — without which no one can buy or sell. Its number, 666, is the number of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Local notables ran the imperial cult, and refusing it cost a tradesman his living.

Now: The mark is an allegiance, not a device; nobody takes it by accident. Test teachers by what they say, not by how familiar they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and it spoke like a dragon. It exercises all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and makes the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second beast rises from the earth, with horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon, and makes the world worship the first beast.

A lamb that speaks like a dragon. Deception: religion that looks gentle and serves the beast.

The false prophet. His name later (16:13; 19:20).

In John’s day. The priests and councils that promoted emperor worship in Asia.

Where Christians differ. Some identify the second beast with a single future religious leader. Verdict: it is false religion or ideology serving state power in every age, with a final climax.
verseByVerse.note: This second beast is later called “the false prophet.”

verseByVerse.quote: It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in front of people, and by the signs that it is allowed to work in the presence of the beast it deceives those who dwell on earth, telling them to make an image for the beast that was wounded by the sword and yet lived. And it was allowed to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might even speak and might cause those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast performs great signs, even calling down fire, and deceives the world into making an image of the first beast, then gives it breath so that it speaks and has non-worshippers killed.

Fire from heaven. A counterfeit of Elijah (and of the two witnesses, 11:5).

Signs can deceive. Miracles are not proof of truth (Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9).

The image. Like Nebuchadnezzar’s statue (Daniel 3).

On a Tuesday. Test every impressive thing by the word of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Also it causes all, both small and great, both rich and poor, both free and slave, to be marked on the right hand or the forehead, so that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second beast forces everyone to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, so that no one can buy or sell without the mark, the beast’s name or number.

A counterfeit seal. God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (7:3; 14:1). The beast copies it.

Hand and forehead. What you do and what you think (Deuteronomy 6:8).

Buy or sell. The pressure of economic exclusion. In Asia, trade guilds required worship of their gods.

What it does not mean. The mark is not a barcode, microchip, credit card or vaccine. Every generation has guessed its own new technology, and all have been wrong. The mark is allegiance.

On a Tuesday. What will it cost you to refuse the world’s worship at work?

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is needed to calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man: 666.

Gematria. In Hebrew and Greek, letters doubled as numbers.

Where Christians differ: what does 666 mean? Many identify Nero: “Nero Caesar” in Hebrew letters adds up to 666, and the Latin form to 616. Others see 666 as falling short of the perfect 7 three times over, the number of humanity trying to be God. Verdict: both may be intended: Nero as the first readers’ example of the beast, and a symbol of human power claiming divinity and always falling short.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read 616. Irenaeus knew this reading in the second century and rejected it. 666 is the better reading.

What it does not mean. Not a code to calculate a modern politician’s name. Such guesses have always failed.

For worship. Thank God that the beast’s number is a man’s, and the Lamb’s name is God’s.
verseByVerse.note: Letters also served as numbers. Many think 666 spells “Neron Caesar” (the Greek form) in Hebrew letters; some manuscripts read 616, which fits the Latin spelling of the name. Others see 666 as falling short of seven again and again.
