22.title: Come, Lord Jesus: The River, the Tree, and the Final Invitation
22.overview:
The final chapter of Revelation — and of the entire Bible — has the quality of a great symphony resolving into its final chord. Everything that has been promised, everything that has been anticipated, every thread of the biblical story, gathers here and arrives. The river of the water of life. The tree of life with twelve kinds of fruit. The servants of God seeing his face. His name on their foreheads. No more night. And then, three times: ‘I am coming soon.’ And the great response of the church across all the ages: ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’

The chapter is framed by the river and tree (vv. 1–5) and the final testimony and invitation (vv. 6–21). The garden returns — but infinitely elevated. Eden had a river flowing from it (Genesis 2:10); the new Jerusalem has a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. Eden had the tree of life (Genesis 2:9); the new Jerusalem has the tree of life bearing twelve kinds of fruit, one each month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in the garden is restored in the city, but the city is greater than the garden: the tree is no longer guarded by cherubim with flaming swords (Genesis 3:24) — it stands in the middle of the street, its fruit available to all.

The closing testimony of the book weaves together three voices: the angel confirming the truth of what has been shown, Jesus speaking in the first person (‘I, Jesus, have sent my angel...’; ‘I am coming soon’), and the Spirit and Bride together issuing the great invitation: ‘Come.’ The book ends not with explanation but with longing — the longing of the church for her Lord, the longing of the Lord for his people, the longing of the Spirit for the consummation of all things. This is the last word of the Bible, and it is the word the whole church has been praying for two thousand years: Come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The River and the Tree of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the middle of the street; and on either side of it the tree of life, bearing twelve crops a year, and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (cf. Ezek. 47:1–12). The Bible has been away from a river and a tree since Genesis 3, where cherubim with a flaming sword were set to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 2:9–10; 3:24). The promise made to Ephesus in the first letter (2:7) is being kept.

Verse 3: No longer will there be anything accursed — the sentence of Genesis 3:17–19 lifted — but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. Verse 4: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. Verse 5: no night, no need of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The River and the Tree

The river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and the tree of life stands open with fruit every month and leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, and his servants will see his face.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The way to the tree, guarded since Eden, stands open in the middle of the street.

Now: Heaven is not first a place but a face — seen at last, and lived through.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb down the city’s street, with the tree of life on both sides, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations. What was lost in Eden is restored and surpassed: unending life flows from God and the Lamb, and the divided nations are tended and made whole.

A river and a tree. Genesis 2 has a river flowing out of Eden and “the tree of life… in the midst of the garden” (Genesis 2:9–10). Genesis 3 ends with the man and woman put out and cherubim “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). From that verse to this one, nobody eats from it. The whole of Scripture happens between a tree being fenced off and a tree being handed back.

A promise kept. Ephesus was told, “To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God” (2:7). Here is the tree.

Better than Eden. This isn’t simply Eden reopened. Eden was a garden; this is a garden inside a city, the river running down the middle of the street. Eden had one tree of life; here it stands “on either side of the river” — impossible to draw, easy to understand: wherever you walk, it is on both sides of you. Eden could be lost; this can’t. God doesn’t restore his people to where they started. He takes them somewhere better, and the road ran through a cross.

From the throne. “Flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” — one throne, two names, no explanation. And what flows from it isn’t judgment but water. Ezekiel saw it: water trickling from under the temple threshold, deepening into a river no one could cross, with trees on both banks whose leaves wouldn’t wither (Ezekiel 47:1–12).

No off season. “Yielding its fruit each month.” Anyone who grows things knows fruit trees rest; there are months with nothing on them. This one doesn’t stop. The life of the city is continually supplied, not merely started.

Healing of the nations. A puzzle, rightly: there is no sickness here, and pain has just been abolished. Ezekiel is the source: “Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing” (Ezekiel 47:12). The word can mean care and tending as much as cure. The most natural sense isn’t that anyone is ill but that the nations are kept well. And “nations” has been a hostile word all book — they raged, drank Babylon’s wine, served the beast. Here they are the ones tended. The long wound of human history — peoples divided at a tower and at each other’s throats ever since — has leaves growing for it. A test: whose people do you find it hardest to love? God is growing leaves for them; pray for them now.
verseByVerse.note: Eden’s river and tree of life return, now in a city.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light, and they will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing accursed will remain; God’s throne and the Lamb’s will be in the city; his servants will worship him, see his face, bear his name, live in his light without night, and reign forever. The curse of Genesis is lifted through Christ, and the heart of heaven is this: God’s people will see his face.

The curse lifted. “No longer will there be anything accursed” reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible: “cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you… till you return to the ground” (Genesis 3:17–19). Everything hard about human life — exhausting labour, resisting ground, failing body — has stood under that sentence. And it is lifted — not managed or explained but removed, because Christ redeemed us “by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). Two trees end this book. On one the curse was absorbed; from the other the fruit is handed out twelve times a year.

The throne in the city. The fixed point of the vision since chapter 4 has always been in heaven. Now it is “in it” — in the city, on the renewed earth, at the end of the street with the river running from it.

They will see his face. Five words, and nothing in Scripture is bigger. Moses, who spoke with God as a friend, asked for exactly this and was told, “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was put in a cleft of the rock and shown God’s back. The high priest went behind the veil once a year and saw nothing. Isaiah saw the train of a robe and cried that he was lost. In chapter 6 kings begged mountains to hide them “from the face of him who is seated on the throne” (6:16). And here, without ceremony: they will see his face. Ordinary people — a slave from Laodicea, a widow from Thyatira, a man who once denied Christ in a courtyard — looking at God, and living.

What heaven is. John wrote the same promise in a letter and admitted he couldn’t fill it in: “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Jesus: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). That is what heaven is. Not a location with good weather; not a reunion, though there will be one; not the end of trouble, though trouble ends. It is a face. The gold, jewels, river and open gates are furniture in a room where that is happening. A test: is seeing God the thing you most long for? Ask him to make it so — and seek his face in prayer today.

His name on their foreheads. The last marked foreheads in the book, and the counterfeit is gone. The seal of 7:3, the Lamb’s name at 14:1, the beast’s mark at 13:16 all led here: everyone is labelled, and these are labelled with him.

Light and reign. No night, no need of lamp or sun, “for the Lord God will be their light” — said twice in eight verses (21:23–25), John’s underlining. And the last word is “reign”: the promise to Laodicea, the weakest church on the road, arriving in full.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6–7: the vision is over and the book begins closing itself by matching its own opening — the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place (cf. 1:1). Then the speaker changes without warning: And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book — the sixth beatitude, almost word for word the first one at 1:3.

Verses 8–9: John falls down to worship the angel a second time and is stopped a second time, in almost the words of 19:10 — I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.

Verses 10–11: Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near — the exact reverse of what Daniel was told (Dan. 12:4, 9) — followed by the hardest verse in the chapter: Let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.

Verses 12–13: the second I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done (cf. Isa. 40:10), and three pairs of titles: Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. Verses 14–15: the seventh and last beatitude — Blessed are those who wash their robes — and the list of those outside, ending with everyone who loves and practices falsehood. Verse 16: I, Jesus, have sent my angel… I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Testimony of Jesus

The book closes as it opened: blessed is the one who keeps its words. The angel refuses John’s worship again — Worship God. The book is left unsealed, for the time is near. Jesus, the Alpha and Omega, root and descendant of David, the bright morning star, is coming soon; blessed are those who wash their robes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole vision was given for the churches, to be read aloud in small rooms.

Now: While the door is open, ask which way your life is already heading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "These words are trustworthy and true. And the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, has sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place." "And behold, I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel affirms that these words are trustworthy and true, sent by the God of the prophets to show his servants what must soon take place; and Christ declares, “I am coming soon. Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.” Revelation is God’s reliable word, completing the prophets, and its blessing rests on those who obey it, not those who merely decode it.

Matching the letterhead. The vision is over; the book now closes itself by returning to its first sentence: “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place” (1:1), made known by his angel to his servant John. Same chain of custody, same phrase, same servants.

The God of the prophets. “The God of the spirits of the prophets” says that the God who spoke through Isaiah, Ezekiel and Daniel — quoted on nearly every page — has spoken here. Revelation isn’t a new departure but the last chapter of a document in progress for fifteen centuries.

“I am coming soon.” The speaker changes without warning: the angel has been talking, and suddenly it is Christ. He says it three times in this chapter (vv. 7, 12, 20), the drumbeat the book ends on.

Soon, after two thousand years? The difficulty is the same as at 1:1 and deserves the same honest answer: the word concerns speed and certainty, not the calendar; the New Testament dates nearness from the cross; and much of what this book describes arrived within its first readers’ lifetimes. And Peter answered this very objection while it was fresh: “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you” (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay isn’t indifference. It is mercy, and someone is being brought in during it.

Keep it. The sixth of the seven blessings, almost word for word the first (1:3). The book opens and closes with a blessing on the same person — not the one who understands it, charts it or identifies the beast, but the one who keeps it. A test: what has Revelation told you to do — endure, hold fast, refuse compromise, worship, come out of Babylon? Pick one and keep it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw them, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed them to me, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John falls down to worship the angel who showed him these things and is stopped again: “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant… Worship God.” Even an apostle overwhelmed by glory can misdirect his worship; the whole book comes down to this command — worship God alone.

Again. He did it at 19:10 and was stopped in nearly these words; here at the very end, with the correction in his own manuscript three chapters back, he goes down a second time. Not flattering to John, and he wrote it down anyway — itself a kind of testimony. He isn’t presenting himself as a man who learned his lesson. That is a comfort to anyone who has repeated a fault he had already repented of: the last recorded act of the apostle who wrote this book is a mistake he had made before. Repent again, and get up.

Undone by beauty. Not at the dragon, beast or lake of fire, but right after the river, the tree and the face. Beauty undoes him. The instinct is right; only the direction is wrong — a man overwhelmed by glory reaches for the nearest thing holding it.

Worship God. Among the shortest complete instructions in Scripture. Twenty-two chapters of visions, and this is the summary.

Alongside the reader. The angel’s self-description is longer than at 19:10: a fellow servant with John, with the prophets, and — new — “with those who keep the words of this book.” That last group is the reader. An angel of God puts himself in the same category as an ordinary Christian who reads Revelation and does what it says.

A permanent danger. Given twice for emphasis. Those through whom God speaks — preachers, writers, movements, teachers — are always at risk of receiving what belongs to God, and most when what they bring is genuinely glorious. The remedy isn’t to think less of the messenger. It is two words. A test: is there someone whose voice you trust more than God’s word? Thank God for them — and worship him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is told not to seal the prophecy, for the time is near; and “let the evildoer still do evil… and the holy still be holy.” Revelation is an open book meant to be read and obeyed now, and there comes a point when a person’s chosen direction becomes permanent — so the time to turn is today.

Unsealed. The reverse of Daniel, who was told to “shut up the words and seal the book, until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:4). John is told to leave it open, because for Daniel the time was far off and for John it is near. And the reverse of 10:4, when John was told, “Seal up what the seven thunders have said.” There is one sealed sentence in Revelation, and we don’t have it. Everything else is open on purpose. So the book isn’t a locked document awaiting a key, and never was. Its blessing falls on the one who keeps it, not the one who cracks it.

The hardest verse. “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.” Read carelessly it sounds like God shrugging — a permission slip for wickedness and a fatalistic verdict that no one changes. Three things settle it.

Its position. It sits between “the time is near” and “I am coming soon” — bracketed by urgency, the opposite of fatalism. Ezekiel was given a similar word when Israel had stopped listening (Ezekiel 3:27), and Daniel too (Daniel 12:10).

Its form. A prophetic announcement, not a divine permission: a moment comes after which character is fixed, when a person’s direction of travel becomes his destination. Everyone knows this of habits within a lifetime; the verse says it is finally true of lives.

What it does to the reader. It isn’t an instruction to the evildoer. It is set before someone holding a book that is nearly finished, and it asks: which of those four describes the direction you are already going? The door is open now, and the invitation is six verses away — “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” — but it won’t be open forever. Read so, v. 11 isn’t God abandoning anyone. It is the most serious way of saying “today.” A reader frightened by it is frightened in exactly the direction it intends, while there is still time to move. Which direction are you facing? Turn now if you must.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel was told to seal his book until the end; John is told not to, because the time is near.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ says he is coming soon, bringing his reward to repay each person for what they have done, and declares himself the Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Christ, who is fully God, will come with his reward in hand, and every faithful deed his grace produced will be remembered.

Reward in hand. The second of three announcements, with the reward already in his hand: “bringing my recompense with me” — not sent for afterwards or calculated on arrival. Isaiah said it of God’s coming: “behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him” (Isaiah 40:10; cf. 62:11).

Each one. “To repay each one for what he has done.” Raised at Thyatira (2:23) and the great white throne (20:12), and the answer hasn’t moved. A record has never admitted anyone, and never failed to identify anyone. It is the evidence of whose a person is and the measure of what is handed him afterwards. And “each one”: nothing is averaged. The visits no one recorded, the giving that hurt, the cup of cold water — each, by name.

Nothing to bring? A fear keeps quiet Christians awake. Someone converted at sixty, or a woman ill in a back bedroom for twenty years, reads “repay each one for what he has done” and thinks there is nothing of theirs to bring. Two things answer. First, what is repaid isn’t what you achieved but what Christ produced in you, and he doesn’t fail to produce — the vine bears the fruit; the branch carries it (John 15:5). Second, Christ told a parable about exactly this: the workers hired at the eleventh hour were paid the same as those who bore the heat of the day, and the owner wronged no one (Matthew 20:1–16). No one will stand there feeling short-changed, and no one thinking he earned what he holds. A test: is your service to Christ driven by fear of having too little, or by love for the One who gives the reward?

Three pairs. “Alpha and Omega” was said by God at 1:8 and 21:6. “The first and the last” was said by the risen Christ at 1:17, and it is Isaiah’s exclusive divine self-description: “I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god” (Isaiah 44:6). “The beginning and the end” completes it. The titles move between Father and Son without a seam, and that isn’t carelessness. Revelation never argues for Christ’s deity; it speaks as though the question couldn’t arise. The One coming soon with his reward was there before history’s first letter and will be there after its last.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates. Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those who wash their robes, for they have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates; outside are the dogs, sorcerers, sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and all who love and practise falsehood. Entry into God’s city comes by being washed in Christ’s blood, and those who cling to sin and love lies remain shut out.

The last blessing. The seventh and last, landing on the one act the whole book describes. Not those who understood it, nor those who suffered, though many did. “Blessed are those who wash their robes” — and 7:14 said in what: “they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

A manuscript detail. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “those who do his commandments” (the King James reading). In Greek the two are startlingly close — hoi poiountes tas entolas autou against hoi plunontes tas stolas autōn — and a tired copyist could slip from one to the other. The earliest and best manuscripts read “wash their robes,” which the ESV follows and the imagery of the book requires. It matters more than most footnotes, because one makes entry depend on obedience and the other on being washed; the manuscripts favour the second, and so does every page from chapter 5 on.

What was lost, given back. “The right to the tree of life” — guarded by a flaming sword since Genesis 3:24, now theirs by right, not trespass. “That they may enter the city by the gates” — a strangely ordinary phrase after everything: not carried in or admitted by a side door, but walking through the front gates like a citizen coming home. A test: are you washed? If you are, walk in as a citizen, not a trespasser — with confidence in prayer today.

Dogs. Not a term of affection: scavengers in the street, a word the law used for what was excluded from the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 23:18), and Paul for those who added requirements to the gospel (Philippians 3:2).

Where is “outside”? Not a place beside the city where the lost live on in sight of it. It is the lake of fire, the second death (20:15; 21:8, 27), described in the language of a city wall: those who won’t enter are shut out.

Loving falsehood. The list ends as every such list in this book ends: “everyone who loves and practices falsehood.” Not merely tells lies — loves them. The dragon is the deceiver of the whole world (12:9), and of the redeemed: “in their mouth no lie was found” (14:5). At the very end, the line between the two companies runs through whether a person loved the truth.
verseByVerse.note: The last of the seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation. Some manuscripts read “do his commandments” for “wash their robes” (ESV note) — the reading of the King James Version.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself declares that he has sent his angel to testify these things for the churches, and that he is the root and descendant of David, the bright morning star. The whole book is the personal word of the human and divine Jesus to ordinary churches, and he himself is the dawn that ends the night.

“I, Jesus.” The name at last — the only place he says it in the book, after twenty-one chapters of titles: the Lamb, the faithful witness, the first and the last, the Word of God, King of kings. At the end he uses the name his mother used, the human name of a carpenter’s son from a village.

For the churches. Not for scholars, a final generation, or the curious. This enormous vision — thrones, dragons, bowls, a city fourteen hundred miles high — was produced for congregations, to be read aloud in rooms. The book ends where it began (1:11), with seven small assemblies on a postal road in Asia. A test: do you read Revelation as a puzzle about others, or as Christ’s letter to your church?

Root and descendant. Both at once, deliberately impossible. To be David’s descendant is to come after him — the promised son of the royal line, born in David’s town. To be David’s root is to be what David grew from; a root isn’t produced by the tree, it produces the tree. Jesus set that riddle himself in the temple, and no one answered it: “David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” (Mark 12:37). This verse is the answer, from the One who asked: David’s son by birth and David’s Lord by nature, one person.

The bright morning star. A promise made twenty chapters ago is identified. Thyatira — the church in the least important town on the road, told only to hold on until he came — was promised “the morning star” (2:28), never explained. It is himself. Behind it stands Balaam’s prophecy, of all people: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (Numbers 24:17).

The last star before dawn. The morning star rises last, when the sky is darkest and the night has gone on longest. It doesn’t announce more night; it means the sun is on its way. That is what this book has said to frightened congregations from its first page. It never promises the dark will be short. It promises who is standing in it. Whatever night you are in, look for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 17: The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (cf. Isa. 55:1; John 4:14; 7:37). Verses 18–19: the covenant scribe’s closing warning against adding to or taking from the words of the prophecy (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5–6), with penalties that fit the offences exactly.

Verse 20: He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” — the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible — and the church’s answer, Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! Verse 21: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come

The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come”; whoever hears is to say it too; whoever is thirsty may take the water of life without price. The book is not to be added to or taken from. Jesus says, “Surely I am coming soon,” and the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The earliest church prayed Marana tha — Our Lord, come.

Now: The most terrifying book in Scripture ends with grace, offered to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit and the Bride say, "Come." And let the one who hears say, "Come." And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit and the Bride say “Come,” and everyone who hears is to say “Come”; let the thirsty come, and whoever desires take the water of life freely. At the end of the Bible’s most frightening book stands its widest invitation: the free gift of eternal life to anyone who wants it, proclaimed by the Spirit through the church.

The last invitation. After the dragon, the beast, the lake of fire and the great white throne, the second-to-last thing God says to the human race is: come and have a drink. The sentence is built like a chain; take it in order.

The Spirit and the Bride. The Holy Spirit and the church speaking together, one verb between them. That is the church’s whole mission in five words, and it settles the relationship: the church doesn’t invite on its own authority, and the Spirit doesn’t work around the church.

The hearer says it too. The invitation is handed on. Whoever has heard it becomes one of those saying it — no interval, no qualification, not the mature or the trained. The one who has just heard is immediately in the chorus. A test: who will you say “Come” to this week? Name them, and invite them.

The thirsty come. Now the direction reverses: the first clauses are the church calling out; this one is someone walking in. The only qualification in the whole verse is thirst — not worthiness, understanding or improvement. Wanting it is the entrance requirement.

Without price. The last clause replaces even “thirsty,” which might sound like a condition, with “the one who desires” — whoever will. And the price is the word of 21:6: as a gift, for nothing. Isaiah shouted it centuries before: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). Jesus shouted it at the feast: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37), and said it quietly to a woman at a well at noon (John 4:14).

Where it is placed. Two verses earlier the dogs and murderers are outside the gate; one verse later comes a solemn warning. In between, unfenced, is the freest offer in Scripture. That is the last word on the character of the God who has run this whole book: the One whose judgments filled sixteen chapters ends by holding out a cup and asking nothing for it.

Does “let the one who desires” mean that salvation depends on our will? The offer is free and open to all, and anyone who comes will receive. But a fallen heart doesn’t thirst for God unaided; the thirst itself is the Spirit’s work drawing people to Christ (John 6:44). The invitation is real, and so is the grace that makes people want to come.

The question of 20:15 answered. Whether a name is in the book of life isn’t settled by “Have I done enough?” — no one has. It is whether a person is thirsty and will come and take what is handed him for nothing. If you are thirsty, come today.

verseByVerse.quote: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book, and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warns that anyone who adds to this book’s words will receive its plagues, and anyone who takes away from them will lose their share in the tree of life and the holy city. God’s word must be received exactly as given — neither supplemented with our speculations nor trimmed of what we dislike.

A covenant seal. Severe, and not unprecedented. It is the standard closing formula of an ancient covenant document, used by Moses: “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2; cf. 12:32; Proverbs 30:5–6). John does what a covenant scribe did when the text was finished: seals it against tampering.

Not a ban on scholarship. Comparing manuscripts to establish what John wrote is the opposite of tampering; it is the effort to ensure nothing has been added or lost. The ESV’s footnote at v. 14 is that work done honestly and in the open.

This book. John says “this book” four times in two verses and means the one he has just finished. The principle plainly extends to Scripture as a whole, and the church has always applied it so; but the verse isn’t a note about the canon.

Adding and taking away. It targets a live danger in every century: people who take a prophecy and improve it. Adding is supplying what God didn’t say — the date, the identity, the extra requirement, the private revelation that completes what Scripture left open. Taking away is removing what he did say — quietly setting aside the judgment, the exclusivity, or the return, because it is unpopular. And the penalties fit exactly: add to the words, and the plagues are added to you; take away from them, and the tree and the city are taken from you. Each person receives the operation he performed.

Can a true believer lose his salvation by taking away from this book? The warning describes those who falsify God’s word, and shows that such people never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19). For believers it is a solemn reason to handle Scripture with reverence, and one of the means God uses to keep them faithful.

A private application. Few readers will publish an edition of Revelation. Many are tempted to do privately what the verse forbids publicly — add a chart the text doesn’t authorise, or subtract the parts that are hard to hear. The instruction of this book from start to finish has been to keep its words: neither more nor less than what is written. A test: which part of this book have you quietly subtracted because it is hard? Read it again, and receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming soon." Amen. Come, Lord Jesus! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ says, “Surely I am coming soon,” the church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”, and the Bible ends: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.” The church lives between the comings by longing and praying for Christ’s return, and the last word of the most terrifying book in Scripture is grace.

His last words. The third and last announcement, and the last recorded words of Jesus Christ in the Bible. Not a command, warning or doctrine, but a promise about arriving. Everything he is has been unfolded over twenty-two chapters — the one who walks among the lampstands, the slain and standing Lamb, the rider with the sword from his mouth, David’s root and offspring, the morning star — and the last thing he says is that he is on his way and won’t be long.

Did Jesus mean “Surely I am coming soon” after two thousand years? “Soon” means his coming is the next great event, near and sudden, not that it would come within a set time. Peter explains the delay: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his patience gives time for repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9). The right response is the church’s prayer.

Maranatha. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” The church answers, barely a sentence: agreement and request. In Aramaic, which these congregations prayed in before Greek took over, it was one word, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come,” which Paul dropped untranslated into a letter to Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22) — a prayer people already said without explanation. That is the church’s state between the comings, and the answer to everything the book has shown. Not a strategy or a timetable, but a prayer that Someone would come, said by people who can’t make him come and are certain he will.

A gentle test. Someone who says “Come, Lord Jesus” and means it has nothing here he would be unwilling to have interrupted. That isn’t a rebuke to anyone who finds the prayer harder than expected; it is simply what the prayer measures. Revelation was written to people who could say it because they had already lost most of what one might want to keep. Pray it today, and notice what in you resists.

The last word is grace. Consider what this book contained: four horsemen, a third of mankind dead, a dragon waiting to devour a child, a beast over every nation, bowls of undiluted wrath, a city drunk on the saints’ blood burned in an hour, a great white throne with no place for earth or sky. By a distance the most terrifying document ever written. And the last word is grace — the word Paul ended every letter with, unearned favour to people with nothing to bring, extended here “with all,” and one more Amen: it is firm, it is so.

So the Bible closes. It opened with a garden, a river and a tree, and a man and woman walking with God; it closes with a city, a river and a tree, and a countless multitude from every nation looking at his face. Between them lies all of human history, and at its centre a Lamb standing as though slain, who took the scroll no one else was worthy to open, and opened it. He is the first and the last; he died and is alive forevermore, holding the keys of Death and Hades (1:18). He is coming soon. And the last thing he leaves his church, after everything, is grace.
verseByVerse.note: “Come, Lord Jesus” matches the Aramaic prayer Maranatha that Paul quotes.

I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”<sup>10</sup>And he said to me, “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.<sup>11</sup>Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy, and the righteous still do right, and the holy still be holy.”<sup>12</sup>“Behold, I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.<sup>13</sup>I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”<sup>14</sup>Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and that they may enter the city by the gates.<sup>15</sup>Outside are the dogs and sorcerers and the sexually immoral and murderers and idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.<sup>16</sup>“I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you about these things for the churches. I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star.”<sup>17</sup>The Spirit and the Bride say, “Come.” And let the one who hears say, “Come.” And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.<sup>18</sup>I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book,<sup>19</sup>and if anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his share in the tree of life and in the holy city, which are described in this book.<sup>20</sup>He who testifies to these things says, “Surely I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!<sup>21</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen.

15.title: The Song of Moses and the Lamb
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the shortest chapter in Revelation — eight verses — but it is one of the most carefully constructed. It serves as the vestibule to the seven bowl visions of chapter 16, doing what chapters 4–5 did before the seals and what chapters 8:1–5 did before the trumpets: grounding the coming sequence in the worship and sovereignty of God before a single bowl is poured. Before heaven acts in judgment, heaven first breaks into song.

The chapter presents two contrasting scenes held in deliberate tension. The first (vv. 1–4): the victorious on the sea of glass, harps in hand, singing the Song of Moses and the Lamb. The second (vv. 5–8): seven angels emerge from the heavenly temple dressed for a solemn task, given seven golden bowls by one of the four living creatures, while the temple fills with the glory of God so completely that no one can enter until the seven bowls are finished. Praise and solemn purpose belong together. The song is not premature celebration; it is the theological foundation without which the coming acts of God would be misread.

The Song of Moses and the Lamb is one of the richest theological moments in the book. It binds together the two great saving acts of God — the Exodus and the cross — into a single song of praise. The God who opened the Red Sea is the God who opened the tomb. The Lamb who was slain is the LORD who drowned Pharaoh’s army. The song the victorious sing is drawn almost entirely from the Psalms, Jeremiah, and Deuteronomy — the whole Hebrew Scripture gathered into the church’s final praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of the Victorious
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: another sign in heaven, great and amazing — the third and last of the book’s three signs, after the woman (12:1) and the dragon (12:3). Seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished. The verb is from teleō, the same root as the word from the cross, It is finished (John 19:30).

Verse 2: the sea of glass of 4:6 is now mingled with fire, and standing beside it are those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, holding harps — a direct contradiction of 13:7, where the beast was allowed to conquer them. The position is the far shore of the Red Sea with Egypt behind it.

Verses 3–4: they sing the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb — one song under two names. Its words are not from Exodus 15 but are a mosaic of Scripture: Great and amazing are your deeds (Ps. 111:2), Just and true are your ways (Deut. 32:4), Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? (Jer. 10:7), All nations will come and worship you (Ps. 86:9). Four clauses, and every one is about God — not one word about the beast, the persecution, or their own endurance.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Song of Moses and the Lamb

Seven angels hold the last plagues, and with them God’s wrath is finished — it has an end, as his mercy does not. Beside the sea of glass, those who conquered the beast sing one song of Moses and the Lamb, made of Scripture and entirely about God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those the beast conquered in the street are standing on the far shore with harps.

Now: Faithfulness that consists in refusing to bow still counts as conquering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees another great sign: seven angels with the last seven plagues, which complete God’s wrath.

The last. The bowls are the final cycle, bringing God’s judgment to completion.

Finished. God’s wrath is not endless rage; it has a purpose and an end.

Plagues. Echoes of Egypt again.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John sees a sea of glass mixed with fire, and beside it those who conquered the beast, holding harps of God.

The sea of glass. Before the throne (4:6). Like Israel beside the Red Sea after crossing it.

Mixed with fire. Judgment, as Pharaoh’s army was judged at the sea.

Conquered. Though killed by the beast (13:7), they won.

For worship. Praise God that his people are brought safely through.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, "Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations! Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, praising the great deeds and just ways of the King of the nations, whom all nations will come and worship.

Moses and the Lamb. Exodus 15. The first exodus pictured the greater one, through Christ.

No word about themselves. The song is entirely about God.

All nations will come. Psalm 86:9. Judgment and mission belong together.

Textual note. Manuscripts read “King of the nations”, “King of the ages”, or (in the King James Version) “King of saints”. The ESV prefers “nations”, which fits the next line.

For worship. Sing to God about God.
verseByVerse.note: As Israel sang beside the sea after the exodus, so God’s redeemed sing after their deliverance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — The Sanctuary Filled with Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 5: the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened. The phrase is the Old Testament’s name for the tabernacle, the tent that housed the ark, which housed the tablets called the testimony because they are God’s witness against a people who agreed to keep them (Ex. 38:21; Num. 1:50). The bowls come out of the place where the covenant is kept.

Verse 6: out come the seven angels, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests — priestly dress (Lev. 16:4; Dan. 10:5), and precisely how the risen Christ was described at 1:13.

Verse 7: one of the four living creatures — the beings nearest the throne, who never cease to say holy, holy, holy — hands over seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God. The word is phialē, a shallow libation dish that empties in a moment, not a jug.

Verse 8: the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement as Liturgy

The bowls come out of the tent of witness, carried by angels in priestly linen and handed over by a worshipper. The golden bowls that once held prayers now hold wrath, and the sanctuary is closed until the plagues are finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The judgement rests on the covenant kept since Sinai.

Now: The sanctuary is open today, with a high priest interceding inside it — pray while it is.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened, and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavenly sanctuary, the tent of witness, is opened, and the seven angels come out dressed in pure bright linen with golden sashes.

The tent of witness. The tabernacle, which held the tablets of the covenant (Exodus 38:21). Judgment proceeds from God’s covenant law.

Dressed as priests. Judgment is holy service.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “stone” (lithon) rather than “linen” (linon). The ESV prefers “linen”, which fits the priestly picture.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever, and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A living creature gives the angels seven golden bowls full of God’s wrath, and the sanctuary fills with smoke from God’s glory, so no one can enter until the plagues are finished.

Golden bowls. The same word as the bowls of the saints’ prayers (5:8). Prayer and judgment are linked.

Smoke. As at the dedication of the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11).

No one could enter. A moment when intercession closes. Now it is still open.

On a Tuesday. The door of mercy stands open today, with a great High Priest inside (Hebrews 7:25). Come now.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I saw another sign in heaven, great and amazing, seven angels with seven plagues, which are the last, for with them the wrath of God is finished.<sup>2</sup>And I saw what appeared to be a sea of glass mingled with fire—and also those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing beside the sea of glass with harps of God in their hands.<sup>3</sup>And they sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!<sup>4</sup>Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.”<sup>5</sup>After this I looked, and the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven was opened,<sup>6</sup>and out of the sanctuary came the seven angels with the seven plagues, clothed in pure, bright linen, with golden sashes around their chests.<sup>7</sup>And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives forever and ever,<sup>8</sup>and the sanctuary was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one could enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished.

16.title: The Seven Bowls: The Completion of Divine Justice
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the third and final series of seven judgments in Revelation, and it is the most intense. Where the seals affected a quarter of the earth and the trumpets a third, the bowls are poured on the whole earth without fraction. The escalation is deliberate: the time for partial warning has passed. These are the last plagues, and with them the response of God to the accumulated rebellion of history reaches its completion.

The bowl series follows the Exodus plague pattern more closely than either the seals or the trumpets. Bowls one through five draw on the Egyptian plagues, though not in their order: sores (bowl 1, cf. Exodus 9:8–11), water turned to blood (bowls 2–3, cf. Exodus 7:17–21), darkness (bowl 5, cf. Exodus 10:21–23). The Exodus pattern is not decorative. It carries a theological message: the God who liberated Israel from Egypt is the same God who now acts in the final Exodus. The pattern of redemptive history repeats at the cosmic scale.

The chapter reaches its climax at the seventh bowl: a loud voice from the throne declares ‘It is done!’ and the greatest earthquake in human history splits the great city into three parts. Babylon is remembered before God and given the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Every island flees, every mountain disappears. The chapter ends not with despair but with the certainty that the one who declared ‘It is done’ from the cross has declared it again from the throne — all things are now moving irresistibly toward the new creation of chapters 21–22.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: a loud voice from the temple — almost certainly God’s own, since 15:8 has just closed the sanctuary to everyone else — orders the seven angels to pour. Verse 2: the first bowl brings harmful and painful sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshipped its image (cf. Ex. 9:8–11).

Verse 3: the sea becomes like the blood of a corpse and everything in it dies — against the second trumpet, which killed a third (8:8–9). Verse 4: the rivers and springs become blood, as the Nile did (Ex. 7:20–21).

Verses 5–7 stop the sequence and defend it. The angel in charge of the waters — whose department has just been ruined — declares Just are you, O Holy One… they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve! And then the altar itself answers: Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!

Verses 8–9: the fourth bowl turns the sun up, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory. Verses 10–11: the fifth falls on the throne of the beast and its kingdom goes dark (cf. Ex. 10:21–23); people gnaw their tongues in anguish and curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores, and did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Ground, Undiluted

The bowls strike earth, sea, rivers, sun and the beast’s throne — the trumpets’ targets, now without limit. The angel of the waters and the altar itself declare God’s judgements true and just. Those struck curse God and do not repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The plagues of Egypt return in one chapter, and the mark becomes the wound.

Now: Suffering drives some to their knees and hardens others; it depends which way a person was already facing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard a loud voice from the temple telling the seven angels, "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God." So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth, and harmful and painful sores came upon the people who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A voice from the temple sends the angels to pour out the bowls of God’s wrath, and the first brings painful sores on those who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image.

The trumpets again, without limits. The bowls strike the same targets as the trumpets, in the same order, but now the whole, not a third. Warning has become final judgment.

Sores. The sixth plague of Egypt (Exodus 9:10–11).

The mark brings the plague. Those who took the beast’s mark now bear its consequences.
verseByVerse.note: The bowls are the last and fullest judgments; unlike the trumpets, they are not limited to a third.

verseByVerse.quote: The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became like the blood of a corpse, and every living thing died that was in the sea. The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of water, and they became blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second bowl turns the sea to blood like a corpse’s, killing everything in it, and the third turns the rivers and springs to blood.

The first plague. The Nile turned to blood (Exodus 7:17–21).

Every living thing. No longer a third (8:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And I heard the angel in charge of the waters say, "Just are you, O Holy One, who is and who was, for you brought these judgments. For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. It is what they deserve!" And I heard the altar saying, "Yes, Lord God the Almighty, true and just are your judgments!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the waters declares God just, for those who shed the blood of saints and prophets are given blood to drink, and the altar answers, “True and just are your judgments.”

Just. The punishment fits the crime.

The altar. Where the martyrs cried “how long?” (6:9–10). Their prayer is answered.

Who is and who was. Again no “who is to come”: he has come.

Textual note. The King James Version reads “and shalt be” in v. 5, from a conjecture by Theodore Beza that has no manuscript support. All manuscripts read “O Holy One”.

For worship. Praise God that his judgments are true and just.

verseByVerse.quote: The fourth angel poured out his bowl on the sun, and it was allowed to scorch people with fire. They were scorched by the fierce heat, and they cursed the name of God who had power over these plagues. They did not repent and give him glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth bowl lets the sun scorch people with fire, and they curse God and refuse to repent.

A reversal. The redeemed were promised the sun would not strike them (7:16).

They cursed God. Suffering does not soften the hardened heart; it reveals it.

On a Tuesday. When trouble comes, it can drive you to God or away from him. Choose to turn towards him.

verseByVerse.quote: The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom was plunged into darkness. People gnawed their tongues in anguish and cursed the God of heaven for their pain and sores. They did not repent of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth bowl plunges the beast’s kingdom into darkness; people gnaw their tongues in pain and curse God, but do not repent.

The throne of the beast. Political power is struck at its centre.

Darkness. The ninth plague (Exodus 10:21–23).

Did not repent. Three times in this chapter (vv. 9, 11, 21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — The Sixth and Seventh Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: the sixth bowl dries the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east — and when Cyrus took Babylon his engineers diverted that river and his troops walked in up the empty bed, exactly as Isaiah had said (Isa. 44:27–28). Verses 13–14: three unclean spirits like frogs (Ex. 8:6) come out of the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet — the unholy trinity together for the first time — and go to the kings of the world to assemble them for battle.

Verse 15 interrupts, in brackets, in Christ’s own voice: Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed! — the third of the book’s seven beatitudes. Verse 16 names the muster point: Armageddon, its only occurrence in the Bible.

Verse 17: the seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from the temple and the throne says It is done! — gegonen, a perfect tense, the completion promised at 15:1. Verse 18: the storm signs at full strength, with an earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth.

Verse 19: the great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. Verse 20: every island flees and no mountains are found (cf. 6:14). Verse 21: hailstones of about a hundred pounds fall (Ex. 9:24) — and they cursed God, for the third time in the chapter, which is the last thing humanity does in it.
verseByVerse.theology:
It Is Done

The Euphrates is dried, and frog-like spirits from the mouths of the dragon, beast and false prophet gather the kings to Armageddon. Christ breaks in: stay awake. The seventh bowl brings the voice from the throne, It is done!, the great earthquake, and Babylon remembered for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Babylon had fallen once before when its river was diverted.

Now: Stay awake and clothed in Christ; ask how much of what you lean on can be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up, to prepare the way for the kings from the east. And I saw, coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs. For they are demonic spirits, performing signs, who go abroad to the kings of the whole world, to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates for the kings from the east, and three unclean spirits like frogs come from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet to gather the kings of the world for battle on the great day of God.

The Euphrates dried. Like the Red Sea and the Jordan, but now to open a way for God’s enemies to their judgment. Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the river.

Where Christians differ: kings from the east. Futurists expect a literal eastern army, often identified with a modern nation. Verdict: John uses his readers’ fear of the Parthians beyond the Euphrates as a picture of all the nations gathered against God.

Frogs. The second plague, and unclean animals (Leviticus 11:10). Deceiving spirits doing signs.

An unholy trinity. Dragon, beast and false prophet: a counterfeit of Father, Son and Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: ("Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!") And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ breaks in: he is coming like a thief, and blessed is the one who stays awake and clothed; and the kings are gathered at the place called Armageddon.

Christ interrupts. In the middle of the gathering of armies, a word to his people: stay awake (3:3, 18).

Blessed. The third of the seven blessings.

Where Christians differ: Armageddon. Many popular writers expect a literal battle at Megiddo in Israel. Verdict: the name means “mountain of Megiddo”, though Megiddo is a plain, not a mountain. It is a symbolic place, recalling famous battles there (Judges 5:19; 2 Kings 23:29): the final gathering of the world against God, which is described in 19:19–21 and 20:8–9. The battle is not fought; it is ended by Christ.

Textual note. Manuscripts spell the name in various ways, including Harmagedon and Mageddon.

On a Tuesday. Keep your garments on: live ready for his coming.
verseByVerse.note: Armageddon probably means “mountain of Megiddo,” a hill fortress overlooking the plain where many of Israel’s famous battles were fought.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, "It is done!" And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a voice from the throne cries, “It is done!”, followed by lightning, thunder and the greatest earthquake ever.

Into the air. The realm of the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2).

It is done. Echoing “It is finished” on the cross (John 19:30), and anticipating 21:6.

The greatest earthquake. The final shaking of all things (Hebrews 12:26–27).

For worship. What Christ finished at the cross, God will finish at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath. And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found. And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great city splits in three, the cities of the nations fall, Babylon drinks the cup of God’s fury, islands and mountains vanish, and huge hailstones fall, yet people curse God.

God remembered Babylon. Her fall is told in chapters 17–18.

Hailstones. About a hundred pounds each. The seventh plague (Exodus 9:24).

Still cursing. The final picture of an unrepentant heart.

The end again. Like the seventh seal and seventh trumpet, the seventh bowl brings the end. The book now looks more closely at it.
