Blessed is the one who stays awake, keeping his garments on, that he may not go about naked and be seen exposed!”)<sup>16</sup>And they assembled them at the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.<sup>17</sup>The seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a loud voice came out of the temple, from the throne, saying, “It is done!”<sup>18</sup>And there were flashes of lightning, rumblings, peals of thunder, and a great earthquake such as there had never been since man was on the earth, so great was that earthquake.<sup>19</sup>The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell, and God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.<sup>20</sup>And every island fled away, and no mountains were to be found.<sup>21</sup>And great hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, fell from heaven on people; and they cursed God for the plague of the hail, because the plague was so severe.

17.title: Babylon the Great: The Seductive City
17.overview:
Chapter 17 introduces one of Revelation’s two great female figures: the great prostitute who sits on many waters, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations. She is the counterpart to the bride of the Lamb (chapters 19 and 21) — two women, two cities, two ways of organising human life. The bride is pure, faithful, clothed in the righteousness of the Lamb. Babylon is seductive, unfaithful, clothed in the luxury of empire. Every human being in history has been drawn toward one or the other.

The identity of Babylon is both specific and universal. In the first century, every reader knew who she was: Rome. The seven hills (v. 9), the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, the city that rules over the kings of the earth (v. 18) — all of this pointed unmistakably to the imperial city on the Tiber. Preterists and idealists agree on this much. Where they differ is on what Rome represents: preterists see primarily the historical Rome of Nero and Domitian; idealists see Rome as the type of every civilisation that organises itself around wealth, power, and the seduction of the nations away from the living God. The idealist position is followed here: Babylon is Rome, and Babylon is every Rome.

The chapter falls into two movements: the vision of the woman on the beast (vv. 1–6) and the angel’s interpretation (vv. 7–18). The interpretation is deliberately cryptic — ‘this calls for a mind that has wisdom’ (v. 9) — and the details about the seven kings and the eighth king have generated more interpretive proposals than almost any other passage in Revelation. The main options are presented honestly here rather than forcing a specific identification that the text itself refuses to make definitive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Woman on the Beast
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–2: one of the bowl angels — tying this chapter to 16:19, where God remembered Babylon — invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters (cf. Jer. 51:13). The kings committed immorality with her; the dwellers on earth merely got drunk on her wine. The same invitation will come from the same rank of angel at 21:9: Come, I will show you the Bride.

Verses 3–4: carried in the Spirit into a wilderness (the Bride is shown from a high mountain, 21:10), John sees a woman riding the scarlet beast of chapter 13 — seven heads, ten horns, blasphemous names. She is arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding a golden cup full of abominations (cf. Jer. 51:7; Matt. 23:25).

Verse 5: a name on her forehead, in a book where that is never incidental (7:3; 13:16; 14:1) — Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations, which the ESV prints in capitals. Verse 6: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus — and John, seeing her, marveled greatly, using the verb this book twice uses of the world’s reaction to the beast (13:3; 17:8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Great Prostitute

John is shown Babylon, magnificent in purple and gold, riding the beast, holding a golden cup full of abominations, drunk with the blood of the saints. She is Rome for the first readers, and the mother of every city built to make a name for itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Kings made the arrangements; ordinary people simply drank what was poured.

Now: The cup always looks better than its contents — and even an apostle had to be asked why he marvelled.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the bowl angels invites John to see the judgment of the great prostitute seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed immorality.

The great prostitute. The prophets called idolatrous cities prostitutes: Nineveh (Nahum 3:4), Tyre (Isaiah 23:17), and Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16).

Immorality. Spiritual unfaithfulness, and the economic and political seduction that goes with it.

Many waters. Peoples and nations (v. 15). Babylon sat on the Euphrates.
verseByVerse.note: “Many waters” recalls ancient Babylon, built on the Euphrates and its canals.

verseByVerse.quote: And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns. The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the wilderness John sees the woman seated on a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup full of abominations.

The best-dressed woman in the world. Purple and scarlet were the costliest dyes, worn by rulers. Babylon is attractive.

A golden cup. Beautiful outside, foul within (Jeremiah 51:7).

Two women. Contrast the woman clothed with the sun (12:1) and the bride clothed in linen (19:8).

On a Tuesday. Babylon does not look evil. It looks rich, glamorous and successful.

verseByVerse.quote: And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: "BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH'S ABOMINATIONS." And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On her forehead is written: “Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations,” and she is drunk with the blood of the saints and of Jesus’ martyrs.

Mystery. A name to be understood spiritually.

Drunk with blood. She persecutes God’s people.

Where Christians differ: who is Babylon? The Reformers, and the Westminster divines, identified her with the papacy and Rome. Others identify her with apostate Jerusalem. Many see the city of Rome in John’s day. Verdict: in John’s day, Rome, the city on seven hills (v. 9). Beyond Rome, she is the world system of pride, luxury and seduction, which recurs in every age. Apostate religion may serve her, but she is broader than any one church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7–8: the angel rebukes the marvelling and explains — and vv. 7 to 18 are the most explicitly interpretive passage in the book, saying this is or these are six times. The beast was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction, and those who marvel at it are those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.

Verses 9–11: this calls for a mind with wisdom — the seven heads are seven mountains and also seven kings, five fallen, one is, one still to come who must remain only a little while; and the beast is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.

Verses 12–14: ten horns are ten kings (cf. Dan. 7:24) who receive authority for one hour and hand their power to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.

Verses 15–16: the waters are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages; and the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire (cf. 2 Kings 9:36; Lev. 21:9). Verse 17: they do it because God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose… until the words of God are fulfilled. Verse 18 closes: the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb Will Conquer

The beast was, and is not — a parody of God’s name — and goes to destruction. The seven kings cannot be identified with certainty, but their time is short. The kings make war on the Lamb and lose, and the beast turns on the woman it carried; God put it in their hearts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those with the Lamb are called, chosen and faithful — in that order.

Now: Evil is not loyal: whatever you ride for safety will one day devour its passengers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to me, "Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel explains the mystery of the woman and the beast that was, is not, and is about to rise from the abyss and go to destruction, and the world marvels at it.

Was, is not, is to come. A parody of God, who was, is and is to come (1:8).

Go to destruction. The beast’s end is certain.

The book of life. Those written in it before the foundation of the world do not marvel at the beast.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “and yet is” instead of “and is to come”.

verseByVerse.quote: This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated; they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while. As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits, and seven kings: five fallen, one living, one still to come for a little while; and the beast is an eighth that belongs to the seven and goes to destruction.

Seven hills. Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

Where Christians differ: the seven kings. Many have tried to count Roman emperors, and it has never worked cleanly. Verdict: seven is the number of completeness. The kings represent the whole succession of world powers, and the beast reappears in a final form before destruction.

This calls for wisdom. Not calculation, but spiritual discernment.
verseByVerse.note: Rome was famous as the city on seven hills.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast. These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast. They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ten horns are ten kings who will reign for one hour with the beast and make war on the Lamb, but the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, with his called, chosen and faithful people.

One hour. Their power is brief.

Lord of lords, King of kings. Deuteronomy 10:17.

Called, chosen and faithful. God’s calling and election, and his people’s faithfulness, together.

For worship. Praise the Lamb who conquers.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages. And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waters are the nations, and the ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute, strip her, devour her flesh and burn her.

Evil turns on itself. The powers that served Babylon destroy her.

Burned. The judgment of an unfaithful priest’s daughter (Leviticus 21:9).

On a Tuesday. The world’s favours are not to be trusted. It devours those who serve it.

verseByVerse.quote: for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled. And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose until his words are fulfilled; and the woman is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.

God’s purpose. Even the plotting of evil powers serves God’s plan (Acts 4:27–28).

The great city. In John’s day, Rome.

For worship. Thank God that no power on earth acts outside his purpose.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and said to me, “Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters,<sup>2</sup>with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality, and with the wine of whose sexual immorality the dwellers on earth have become drunk.”<sup>3</sup>And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names, and it had seven heads and ten horns.<sup>4</sup>The woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and jewels and pearls, holding in her hand a golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her sexual immorality.<sup>5</sup>And on her forehead was written a name of mystery: “BABYLON THE GREAT, MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF EARTH’S ABOMINATIONS.”<sup>6</sup>And I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. When I saw her, I marveled greatly.<sup>7</sup>But the angel said to me, “Why do you marvel? I will tell you the mystery of the woman, and of the beast with seven heads and ten horns that carries her.<sup>8</sup>The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the bottomless pit and go to destruction. And the dwellers on earth whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel to see the beast, because it was and is not and is to come.<sup>9</sup>This calls for a mind with wisdom: the seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman is seated;<sup>10</sup>they are also seven kings, five of whom have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come, and when he does come he must remain only a little while.<sup>11</sup>As for the beast that was and is not, it is an eighth but it belongs to the seven, and it goes to destruction.<sup>12</sup>And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received royal power, but they are to receive authority as kings for one hour, together with the beast.<sup>13</sup>These are of one mind, and they hand over their power and authority to the beast.<sup>14</sup>They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.”<sup>15</sup>And the angel said to me, “The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is seated, are peoples and multitudes and nations and languages.<sup>16</sup>And the ten horns that you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute. They will make her desolate and naked, and devour her flesh and burn her up with fire,<sup>17</sup>for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind and handing over their royal power to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.<sup>18</sup>And the woman that you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.”

18.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon the Great
18.overview:
Chapter 18 is Revelation’s sustained lament over the fall of the great city. It is one of the longest chapters in the book, and it is deliberately literary in character — structured like the great prophetic dirges of the Old Testament (Isaiah 13–14 over Babylon; Ezekiel 26–28 over Tyre; Ezekiel 27 especially, whose cargo list John adapts in vv. 12–13). The chapter uses the Old Testament’s own poetic forms to announce the end of the Old Testament’s great enemy.

The chapter moves through three distinct movements. First (vv. 1–8): the angelic announcement of Babylon’s fall and the call for God’s people to come out of her. Second (vv. 9–20): the threefold lament of the kings, merchants, and seafarers — three groups whose wealth depended on Babylon, each mourning from a safe distance as the city burns. Third (vv. 21–24): the millstone sign and the sixfold silence — the total, irreversible end of the city that made the nations drunk with her wine.

The economic detail of chapter 18 is one of its most striking features. The cargo list of vv. 12–13 is specific, comprehensive, and damning — ending with ‘slaves, that is, human souls.’ Babylon’s economy is built on everything, including people. The city that offered the nations luxury and culture and wealth was also the city that traded in human beings as commodities. This is Revelation’s most direct indictment of the economics of empire, and it is not limited to the Roman slave trade: every economic system that treats human beings as means rather than ends falls under the same indictment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Announcement and the Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1: an angel with great authority comes down and the earth was made bright with his glory (cf. Ezek. 43:2). Verses 2–3: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! — the announcement of 14:8 now given twenty-four verses instead of one. She becomes a haunt of demons and unclean birds, which is exactly what the prophets said of the first Babylon (Isa. 13:21–22; Jer. 50:39). And three groups are named who will structure the chapter: the nations who drank, the kings who traded, and — new here — the merchants, who grew rich from the power of her luxurious living.

Verses 4–5: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues (Jer. 51:45; Isa. 52:11; cf. 2 Cor. 6:17), for her sins are heaped high as heaven — a tower again (Gen. 11:4) — and God has remembered her iniquities.

Verses 6–8: repay her double in the cup she mixed; and Babylon speaks in her own voice, quoted from Isaiah’s taunt against the original city (Isa. 47:7–8): I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see. The three things she says she will never see are the three that arrive: death and mourning and famine, all in a single day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Come Out of Her

Babylon is fallen and left a haunt of unclean things. God’s people are called to come out of her — not by emigrating but by refusing to share her sins. She said she would never see mourning; death, mourning and famine come in a single day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What the beast enforced by law, Babylon sustained by trade.

Now: Coming out of Babylon happens in small daily refusals; beware the unspoken belief that your comforts will simply go on.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory. And he called out with a mighty voice, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast. For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glorious angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons, because the nations, kings and merchants were seduced and enriched by her.

Fallen, fallen. Isaiah 21:9. Announced as already done.

A haunt of demons. The language of ruined cities in the prophets (Isaiah 13:21; Jeremiah 50:39).

Three groups. Nations, kings and merchants: the whole system of power and trade.

Where Christians differ: who is Babylon here? Some expect a rebuilt city of Babylon in Iraq. Verdict: as in chapter 17, Babylon was Rome in John’s day, and is the world system of luxury, power and seduction in every age, which God will finally destroy.

Textual note. Manuscripts differ between “have drunk” (pepōkan) and “have fallen” (peptōkan) in v. 3. The ESV reads “drunk”.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues; for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another voice calls God’s people to come out of Babylon, so as not to share her sins or her plagues, for her sins are heaped to heaven and God has remembered them.

Come out. Jeremiah 51:45; Isaiah 52:11.

What it does not mean. Not leaving the world physically (John 17:15), but refusing its values, idolatry and compromise (2 Corinthians 6:17).

Heaped high. Like the tower of Babel.

On a Tuesday. Where are you sharing in Babylon’s sins, at work, online, with money? Come out.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed. As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.' For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon is to be repaid double for her deeds, given torment to match her self-glory and luxury, because she said, “I sit as a queen; I will never see mourning,” and so her plagues will come in a single day.

Double. A full and fitting repayment (Jeremiah 16:18).

I sit as a queen. Isaiah 47:7–9, Babylon’s boast.

Pride. The root of her sin: self-glorifying security.

Mighty is the Lord God. The one who judges her is stronger.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three sets of mourners in descending rank, modelled on Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre (Ezek. 26–28). Verses 9–11: the kings weep and wail, stand far off, in fear of her torment, and cry Alas! Alas! You great city… For in a single hour your judgment has come; and the merchants mourn since no one buys their cargo anymore.

Verses 12–13 give the manifest: twenty-eight items in seven groups, running downward from precious metals and stones through fabrics, fine furniture, spices, food and livestock — and ending and slaves, that is, human souls. Verse 14 speaks to the city directly: the fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you… never to be found again.

Verses 15–16: the merchants stand far off and describe her as a dressed body — linen, purple, scarlet, gold, jewels, pearls, nearly the wording of 17:4. Verses 17–19: shipmasters, seafaring men and sailors stand far off, throw dust on their heads (cf. Ezek. 27:29–32), and cry What city was like the great city? and in a single hour she has been laid waste.

Verse 20 opens a window in the middle of the funeral: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!
verseByVerse.theology:
The Threefold Lament

Kings, merchants and sailors stand far off and weep — for their trade, not for her. The cargo list ends with slaves, that is, human souls. Heaven and the saints are called to rejoice because God has given judgement for them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole Roman world was arranged to supply one city.

Now: Ask whose hands made what you hold, and whether your deepest grief would be for a person or for a market.

verseByVerse.quote: And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning. They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, "Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come." And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings who shared her immorality and luxury weep over the smoke of her burning, standing far off and crying “Alas!” at her sudden judgment.

Ezekiel 26–27. The lament over Tyre.

Far off. They mourn their loss but do not help her.

One hour. All that glory gone so quickly.
verseByVerse.note: The laments echo Ezekiel’s dirge over the trading city of Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The merchants weep, because no one buys their cargoes any more: precious metals, cloth, spices, food, animals, and slaves, that is, human souls.

The list. Nearly thirty items, from luxuries to necessities, ending with people.

Human souls. The slave trade, the climax of Babylon’s greed. Scripture condemns trading in people (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10).

What it does not mean. Not that trade or wealth is evil in itself. The sin is luxury, idolatry, and treating people as cargo.

On a Tuesday. Ask where your purchases come from, and who pays the price.
verseByVerse.note: The cargo list ends with human beings — the slave trade on which Rome’s economy depended.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!" The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud, "Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fruit she longed for is gone, and the merchants who grew rich from her stand far off, weeping and mourning over the great city clothed in purple and gold.

The fruit your soul longed for. Desires fed by the world are finally lost.

They mourn the money. Their grief is for their own losses.

verseByVerse.quote: For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste." And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, "Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one hour all this wealth is laid waste, and shipmasters and sailors stand far off, throw dust on their heads, and lament the city that made them rich.

Dust on heads. Mourning (Ezekiel 27:30).

What city was like her? The world’s admiration turns to grief.

On a Tuesday. Store up treasure that will not burn (Matthew 6:19–21).

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven, saints, apostles and prophets are called to rejoice, because God has judged her for them.

Victims, not spectators. Those called to rejoice are those she killed (v. 24).

What it does not mean. This is not gloating, but joy that justice is done and the oppressed are vindicated.

For worship. Thank God that the blood of his people will not be forgotten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–24 — The Millstone and the Sixfold Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 21: a mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea — the act Jeremiah commanded of Seraiah, who tied a stone to the scroll of Babylon’s doom and threw it into the Euphrates saying Thus shall Babylon sink, to rise no more (Jer. 51:59–64). A millstone is the heaviest ordinary object in an ancient town and the last thing in the world that floats.

Verses 21–23 toll a sixfold silence, six things heard or found no more: Babylon herself; the sound of harpists and musicians, flute players and trumpeters; a craftsman of any craft; the sound of the mill; the light of a lamp; and the voice of bridegroom and bride. Jeremiah listed the same three — millstones, lamp, bridegroom and bride — as the sum of what a judged city loses (Jer. 25:10). Two reasons are given: your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery (pharmakeia, as at 9:21).

Verse 24 gives the indictment: And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Millstone and the Silence

An angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon sinks. Music, craft, the mill, the lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom are heard in her no more — and in her is found the blood of the prophets and saints.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jeremiah had sunk Babylon’s doom in the Euphrates; John’s angel repeats the sign.

Now: The ordinary goods of life — bread, lamplight, weddings — were always worth more than the cargo. Nothing hidden stays unlooked-for.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, "So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more; and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more, and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery. And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea: so Babylon will be thrown down and never found again, and no music, craft, lamp or wedding will be heard in her, for her merchants were the world’s great ones, her sorcery deceived the nations, and in her was found the blood of prophets and saints.

Jeremiah 51:63–64. A stone thrown into the Euphrates.

No more. Six times. The silence of total ruin.

The ordinary joys gone. Music, work, light, marriage: good gifts lost because they were used without God.

Sorcery. Her deceiving spell.

All who have been slain. Babylon is responsible for the blood of the righteous through all history (Matthew 23:35).

For worship. Praise God that the city of the world will fall, and the city of God will stand.
verseByVerse.note: Jeremiah had a scroll against Babylon tied to a stone and thrown into the Euphrates.

18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was made bright with his glory.<sup>2</sup>And he called out with a mighty voice, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit, a haunt for every unclean bird, a haunt for every unclean and detestable beast.<sup>3</sup>For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living.”<sup>4</sup>Then I heard another voice from heaven saying, “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues;<sup>5</sup>for her sins are heaped high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.<sup>6</sup>Pay her back as she herself has paid back others, and repay her double for her deeds; mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed.<sup>7</sup>As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning, since in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.’<sup>8</sup>For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”<sup>9</sup>And the kings of the earth, who committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her, will weep and wail over her when they see the smoke of her burning.<sup>10</sup>They will stand far off, in fear of her torment, and say, “Alas! Alas! You great city, you mighty city, Babylon! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”<sup>11</sup>And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore,<sup>12</sup>cargo of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple cloth, silk, scarlet cloth, all kinds of scented wood, all kinds of articles of ivory, all kinds of articles of costly wood, bronze, iron and marble,<sup>13</sup>cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls.<sup>14</sup>“The fruit for which your soul longed has gone from you, and all your delicacies and your splendors are lost to you, never to be found again!”<sup>15</sup>The merchants of these wares, who gained wealth from her, will stand far off, in fear of her torment, weeping and mourning aloud,<sup>16</sup>“Alas, alas, for the great city that was clothed in fine linen, in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, with jewels, and with pearls!<sup>17</sup>For in a single hour all this wealth has been laid waste.” And all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off<sup>18</sup>and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, “What city was like the great city?”<sup>19</sup>And they threw dust on their heads as they wept and mourned, crying out, “Alas, alas, for the great city where all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.<sup>20</sup>Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!”<sup>21</sup>Then a mighty angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying, “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more;<sup>22</sup>and the sound of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters, will be heard in you no more, and a craftsman of any craft will be found in you no more, and the sound of the mill will be heard in you no more,<sup>23</sup>and the light of a lamp will shine in you no more, and the voice of bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more, for your merchants were the great ones of the earth, and all nations were deceived by your sorcery.<sup>24</sup>And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.”

19.title: Hallelujah! The Wedding and the Rider
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the great pivot of Revelation — the hinge between Babylon’s fall and the new creation. It opens with the loudest sound in the book: the fourfold Hallelujah chorus of heaven celebrating the justice of God and the arrival of the marriage supper of the Lamb. It closes with the appearance of the Rider on the white horse, whose name is Word of God, whose robe is dipped in blood, who strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth, and who is named King of kings and Lord of lords.

The chapter falls into two movements that mirror each other. The first (vv. 1–10) is pure celebration: heaven erupts in praise, the twenty-four elders and four living creatures worship, the great multitude shouts like the roar of many waters, and the Bride has made herself ready in fine linen bright and pure — the righteous deeds of the saints. The second (vv. 11–21) is the appearing of the Rider: heaven opened, white horse, faithful and true, eyes of flame, many diadems, name unknown, Word of God, armies following, sharp sword from his mouth, King of kings. The beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire.

The relationship between the two movements is crucial. The praise precedes the appearing; the wedding supper is announced before the battle is described. This is Revelation’s consistent pattern: the outcome is declared before the outworking. Heaven celebrates the marriage of the Lamb while the final confrontation with the beast is still being described. The sequence is not chronological; it is theological. The Lamb has already conquered. What the Rider on the white horse depicts is the visible manifestation of a victory already secured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Hallelujah and the Marriage Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1–3: a great multitude cries Hallelujah! — Hebrew, untranslated, the great word of the psalter, and used in the New Testament only in these six verses, four times. The grounds are given: his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute… and has avenged on her the blood of his servants — the two verbs the martyrs asked for at 6:10, now in the past tense. And the smoke from her goes up forever and ever (cf. Isa. 34:10).

Verses 4–5: the elders and living creatures, in their last appearance in the book, fall down and say two Hebrew words — Amen. Hallelujah! (cf. Ps. 106:48). Then a voice from the throne: Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great.

Verses 6–8: the last hallelujah, in a voice like many waters and thunder — the Lord our God the Almighty reigns (cf. Ps. 93:1; 97:1) — and the announcement the book has been travelling toward: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure — for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.

Verses 9–10: the fourth beatitude, and one of the few sentences John is told to write down (cf. 14:13; 21:5) — Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. John falls down to worship the angel and is stopped: You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you… Worship God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hallelujah and the Wedding

Heaven’s hallelujahs answer the martyrs’ prayer: God has judged and avenged. The marriage of the Lamb has come; the Bride is granted fine linen, which is the righteous deeds of the saints. Blessed are those invited — and worship God, not his messengers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The prayer under the altar was not lost; it was answered.

Now: The hidden faithfulness of ordinary believers is being woven into the Bride’s dress.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I heard what seemed to be the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven, crying out, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality, and has avenged on her the blood of his servants." Once more they cried out, "Hallelujah! The smoke from her goes up forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great multitude in heaven cries “Hallelujah!”, praising God because his judgments are true and just, and he has judged the great prostitute and avenged his servants’ blood.

Hallelujah. “Praise the LORD”. The only place in the New Testament where it appears, four times.

Salvation and judgment together. God’s judgment of Babylon is part of his salvation of his people.

Her smoke goes up for ever. Isaiah 34:10.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “and honour” to the ascription in v. 1.
verseByVerse.note: “Hallelujah” means “praise the LORD” (Hebrew). In the New Testament it appears only here, four times in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who was seated on the throne, saying, "Amen. Hallelujah!" And from the throne came a voice saying, "Praise our God, all you his servants, you who fear him, small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders and living creatures worship, saying “Amen. Hallelujah!”, and a voice from the throne calls all God’s servants, small and great, to praise him.

Amen. Heaven agrees with God’s judgments.

Small and great. Every believer is called to praise.

For worship. Answer heaven’s call: praise our God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, "Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns. Let us rejoice and exult and give him the glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready; it was granted her to clothe herself with fine linen, bright and pure"—for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vast multitude roars “Hallelujah!” because the Lord God Almighty reigns, and the marriage of the Lamb has come; his bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints.

He reigns. The fourth Hallelujah. Handel set it.

The marriage of the Lamb. Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:25–27). The prophets pictured God as Israel’s husband (Hosea 2:19–20).

Made herself ready, and it was granted her. Both. The linen is given, and the bride wears it.

Righteous deeds. Not the righteousness that justifies, which is Christ’s alone, but the holy lives that flow from it (Ephesians 2:10).

Two women. The prostitute in purple, the bride in linen.

On a Tuesday. Your acts of righteousness today are part of the bride’s wedding dress.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." And he said to me, "These are the true words of God." Then I fell down at his feet to worship him, but he said to me, "You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold to the testimony of Jesus. Worship God." For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel declares blessed those invited to the Lamb’s marriage supper; John falls to worship the angel, who stops him: worship God, for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

Blessed. The fourth of the seven blessings.

Do not worship angels. Even a glorious angel is a fellow servant (22:8–9; Colossians 2:18). Yet the Lamb is worshipped (5:13): he is God.

The spirit of prophecy. All true prophecy bears witness to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Watch for anything, however good, that draws worship away from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Rider on the White Horse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 11–13: heaven opens — not a door this time — and a rider comes out on a white horse, called Faithful and True (cf. 1:5; 3:14), and in righteousness he judges and makes war (cf. Isa. 11:3–4). His eyes are a flame of fire (1:14); on his head are many diadems, against the dragon’s seven and the beast’s ten; he has a name written that no one knows but himself; he is clothed in a robe dipped in blood; and he is called The Word of God — John’s own title for him (John 1:1).

Verses 14–16: the armies of heaven follow, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure — the Bride’s dress from v. 8, in the same words. From his mouth comes a sharp sword (1:16; Isa. 11:4); he will rule with a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9); he treads the winepress (Isa. 63:3). And on his robe and thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords (cf. Deut. 10:17; Rev. 17:14).

Verses 17–18: an angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God (Ezek. 39:17–20), to eat the flesh of kings, captains, mighty men, horses and riders, both free and slave, both small and great. Verses 19–21: the beast and the kings gather to make war — and the beast was captured, with the false prophet, and both are thrown alive into the lake of fire; and the rest are slain by the sword from the rider’s mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rider on the White Horse

Faithful and True, crowned with many diadems, robed in blood, named the Word of God and King of kings and Lord of lords, the Rider strikes the nations with the sword of his mouth. The beast and false prophet are captured without a battle and thrown into the lake of fire.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The churches had no army; the armies of heaven ride out in wedding clothes and strike no blow.

Now: There are two suppers in this chapter: at one people are guests, at the other they are the meal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes are like a flame of fire, and on his head are many diadems, and he has a name written that no one knows but himself. He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and the name by which he is called is The Word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse appears, called Faithful and True, judging and making war in righteousness, with eyes of fire, many crowns, a secret name, a robe dipped in blood, and the name the Word of God.

The second coming. Christ returns as judge and king.

Not the rider of 6:2. That rider had a bow and was given one crown. This one wears many crowns and wields the word.

Faithful and True. His title to Laodicea (3:14).

Where Christians differ: whose blood? Some see the blood of his enemies (Isaiah 63:1–3), since the robe is bloodied by the winepress (v. 15). Others see his own blood, shed on the cross. Verdict: his robe is bloodied before the battle begins (v. 19), so it is most likely his own blood, by which he has already conquered (5:9; 12:11), though Isaiah’s picture of judgment is also in view.

The Word of God. John 1:1.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “sprinkled with blood” rather than “dipped in blood”.

verseByVerse.quote: And the armies of heaven, arrayed in fine linen, white and pure, were following him on white horses. From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and he will rule them with a rod of iron. He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has a name written, King of kings and Lord of lords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The armies of heaven follow him in white linen; he strikes the nations with the sword from his mouth, rules them with an iron rod, treads the winepress of God’s wrath, and bears the name King of kings and Lord of lords.

The armies. Saints and angels (17:14). They do not fight. Christ alone wins.

The sword of his mouth. His word (Isaiah 11:4; 2 Thessalonians 2:8).

Where Christians differ: does chapter 20 follow in time? Premillennialists read chapter 20 as the next stage: a thousand-year earthly reign after Christ’s return. Verdict: chapter 20 goes back to cover the church age from another angle, as the book does throughout. The battle of 20:7–10 is the same final battle as here (both draw on Ezekiel 38–39).

For worship. Bow before the King of kings and Lord of lords.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and with a loud voice he called to all the birds that fly directly overhead, "Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all men, both free and slave, both small and great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel standing in the sun calls the birds to the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, captains, horses, riders and all people.

Ezekiel 39:17–20. The feast for the birds after God’s defeat of Gog.

Two suppers. The marriage supper of the Lamb (v. 9) or the great supper of God. Everyone attends one of them.

On a Tuesday. Accept the invitation to the Lamb’s supper while it is offered.

verseByVerse.quote: And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies gathered to make war against him who was sitting on the horse and against his army. And the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who in its presence had done the signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur. And the rest were slain by the sword that came from the mouth of him who was sitting on the horse, and all the birds were gorged with their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beast and kings gather to war against the rider, but the beast and false prophet are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from his mouth.

No battle. The armies gather; Christ speaks; it is over.

The lake of fire. Final punishment (20:10, 14–15).

Thrown alive. Conscious punishment.

For worship. Praise Christ, whose word ends all opposition.
